syntax_simple.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest is hindered by modeling issues. Often, the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are not accessible. Sometimes they are known. Their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Approximating complex systems in a generic functional format has become common practice in the age of machine learning. This approach informs the format ex-nihilo from available observations. The numerous successful examples are based on deep neural networks. This is not surprising. However, generalizability of the models is often overlooked. Margins of guarantee are often overlooked. The impact of data is often overlooked. These aspects are examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics. We tackle these issues from a different viewpoint. We adopt a curriculum learning strategy. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured in a particular way. The training process starts from simple samples. It moves towards more complex ones. This favors convergence. This favors generalization. The concept has been developed in robotics. It has been successfully applied in control of systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems. We do this in a systematic way. First, we leverage insights from the ergodic theory. We assess the amount of data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the physical system. We thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set on the quality of long-term predictions. We investigate its structure on prediction quality. Based on that, we consider entropy as a metric of complexity of the dataset. We show how an informed design of the training set significantly improves the resulting models. This design is based on the analysis of the entropy. The improvement is in terms of generalizability. We provide insights on the amount of data required. We provide insights on the choice of data required for effective data-driven modeling.
syntax_simple.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies. Substantial variations are seen from object to object. The main source of the emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood. Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several kpc or more. The observed emission is an average of different ISM components. The aim of this work is to study the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. We do this for the first time. We want to investigate the origin of this line. We want to investigate its use as a tracer of star formation. We present CII and OI observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31. We use the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas. These tracers are CO and HI. The CII emission is compared with tracers of star formation. These tracers are H\alpha and Spitzer 24 mu. The similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24 mu images is striking. They are smoothed to the same resolution. The correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from the border of the map to the regions of star formation. It goes from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom to ~1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom. The CII/FIR(42-122) ratio is almost constant at 2%. This is a factor 3 higher than typically quoted. However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. The whole-galaxy fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions. The CII/FIR ratio is known to be lower there. The resolved observations do not isolate a spiral arm. They do not include data as far out in the galactic disk as the observations presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average solution. The solution is G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR emission. This applies to the regions of star formation in the arm of M31.
syntax_simple.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model. This model describes a topological crystalline insulator (TCI). Rotation symmetry protects it. The model is built by stacking two Chern insulators. These insulators have opposite Chern numbers. They transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group. An example is $p_\pm$ orbitals. The model appears similar to the Kane-Mele model. However, it does not host stable gapless surface states. Nevertheless, the model exhibits topological responses. These responses are important. One response is the appearance of quantized fractional charge. This charge is bound to rotational defects. These defects are disclinations. Another response is the pumping of angular momentum. This pumping occurs in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux. A mutual Chern-Simons coupling describes these responses. This coupling occurs between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field. The effective gauge field corresponds to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show something important about the filled bands of the model. These bands do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation. However, this obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals. This implies fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived. We represent it as a superposition of atomic orbitals. These orbitals have positive and negative integer coefficients. The analysis of the model serves as a prototypical example. This example concerns 2D TCIs protected by rotation. We show that all TCIs protected by point group symmetries follow a pattern. These TCIs do not have protected surface states. They are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. This implies something remarkable. Gapless surface states exist in free electron systems under a specific condition. This condition is the presence of a stable Wannier obstruction. This is true if and only if this obstruction exists. We then use dimensional reduction. This reduction maps the problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem. We use this 0D problem to obtain results. We obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs. We also obtain the reduction of this classification. This reduction occurs in the presence of interactions.
syntax_simple.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach. We call it the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). It uses selected attributes from objects in various domains. These domains include chess problems, classical music, and renowned artworks. The system recombines these attributes in a specific way. It generates new attributes through this process. These new attributes can then be used in principle. They can create novel objects of creative value to humans. These objects relate to any one of the source domains. This allows something important to happen. Some of the burden of creative content generation passes from humans to machines. We tested the approach in the domain of chess problem composition. We used it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems. These problems were based on attributes we extracted and recombined. The sources included chess problems and tournament games by humans. They also included renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. We then assessed the quality of these generated chess problems. We assessed them automatically using an existing computational chess aesthetics model. This model had been experimentally validated. Human experts in the domain also assessed the problems. The results suggest something interesting. Attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains can indeed be used effectively. The DSNS approach enables this. These attributes can automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. One finding stood out in particular. A low quality chess source produced strong results. This source consisted of tournament game sequences between weak players. It was used in combination with actual photographs of people. It was able to produce three-move chess problems. These problems had comparable quality or better. They matched those generated using a high quality chess source. That high quality source consisted of published compositions by human experts. The low quality source was also more efficient. Why can information from a foreign domain be integrated this way? Why is it functional? This remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is scalable in principle. It is applicable to any domain. Objects in that domain must have attributes. These attributes must be representable using real numbers.
syntax_simple.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak appears in the cosmic matter distribution. Observers see it at redshifts up to approximately 3.5. It reflects the continued expansion of the sonic horizon. Scientists first identified this horizon in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. The BAO peak position can now be measured with high accuracy. Galaxies allow measurements to better than approximately 1% accuracy. Ly-alpha forests and the clustering of quasars provide approximately 1.4-1.6% precision. Scientists use the BAO measurement in conjunction with the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP) effect. The AP effect arises from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift size. This ratio changes with distance for source distributions. These distributions are presumed to be spherically symmetric. The BAO measurement is viewed as one of the most powerful tools available. Scientists use it in assessing the geometry of the Universe. In this paper, we employ five BAO peak measurements. These measurements come from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV. The average redshifts are <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33. We carry out a direct head-to-head comparison of two cosmological models. One model is the standard model, Lambda-CDM. The other is one of its principal competitors. This competitor is known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we complement the AP diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe. This probe assumes a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both probes are free of uncertain parameters. The Hubble constant is one such uncertain parameter. These probes are therefore ideally suited for this kind of model selection. We find that R_h=ct is favored by these measurements over the standard model. This conclusion is based solely on the AP effect. The likelihood is approximately 75% versus approximately 25%. Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct based solely on the volume-averaged distance probe. That likelihood is approximately 80% versus approximately 20%. A joint analysis using both probes produces an inconclusive outcome. It yields comparable likelihoods to both models. We are therefore not able to confirm a key conclusion with this work. The BAO data, on their own, do not support an accelerating Universe.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy. They host star formation. We must detect them in a reliable way. This detection is key towards our understanding of the star formation process.

Aims. We explore a question. Can supervised machine learning identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane?

Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks. These networks perform image segmentation. We used H2 column density images of the Galactic plane. Herschel Hi-GAL data provided these images. We used them as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons of filaments. These skeletons included the spine plus branches. We extracted these filaments from the images. We also produced background masks. We produced missing data masks. We tested eight training scenarios. We wanted to determine the best scenario. Our astrophysical purpose was classifying pixels as filaments.

Results. The training of the UNets allows us something. We can create a new image of the Galactic plane. We create it by segmentation. Pixels belong to filamentary structures. We identify these pixels. We classify more pixels with this new method. We classify more by a factor of 2 to 7. This factor depends on the classification threshold used. We classify more pixels as belonging to filaments. We classify more than the spine plus branches structures. We used those structures as input. New structures are revealed. These structures are mainly low-contrast filaments. They were not detected before. We use standard metrics. These metrics evaluate the performances. We evaluate the different training scenarios. This allows us to demonstrate the robustness of the method. We determine an optimal threshold value. This value maximizes the recovery. We recover the input labelled pixel classification.

Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows something. Supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures. These structures are present throughout the Galactic plane. We detect these structures. We detect low-density structures. We detect low-contrast structures. Nobody has seen these structures before. This detection offers important perspectives. These perspectives concern the study of these filaments.

The program can't handle that situation. It may crash. Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. A program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits. The computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. The program can't handle that situation. It may crash. Deadlock: Let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block. Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks. You tell Billy something. You will give him the red block after he gives you the blue block. Billy tells you something. He will give you the blue block after you give him the red block. Both of you will sit there forever. You wait for the other person to hand over their block. You will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation. It happens inside a program. The program freezes up. There is nothing you can do except kill it and start it again. Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. An error is detected. Part of the program throws an exception. Another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. An exception gets thrown. It is not caught by any part of the program. Usually a dialog will pop up. It lets you know that a problem was not dealt with properly. The program will terminate. All of these situations are caused by "bugs" in the program. "Bugs" are just parts of the program. They are not written correctly. They don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more "bugs" than other programs. Why? This paper extends the Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper. It shows CNN representations at the FC7 layer are equivariant to various classes of transformations to a certain extent. It also shows that training with a certain group of transformations makes the representations more equivalent.

The authors performed a large amount of experiments. They trained over 30 networks with different forms of jitter. This is quite impressive. However, it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work. The authors measured the properties on a different layer than Lenc&Vedaldi15. It is hard to find some novel insights beyond this. There is a known fact that jitter helps to achieve invariance. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct. The paper does not seem to solve the task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues appear in the experiments with the representation distances. The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial. It is followed only by a single classification layer. This layer is FC8. FC8 goes to the common output. The common output is class likelihoods. FC8 is just a linear projection. The equivalence map re-projects the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Performing similar experiments on more layers may be more useful. The networks are already trained.

The experiment with representation distance is missing something important. It does not show the classification error on the testing dataset. This would answer a key question. The question is whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all.

It is not clear for the experiment with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example. Is it measured after training the equivalence map? It would be more clear to show that networks trained on similar groups of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task.

The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Lambda_1 and lambda_2 have such small values. The loss is basically equal to simple data jitter. It just adds up the loss of the original image and the transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer.

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance. It does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these experiments. There are some issues with the equivalence experiments. There are also issues with the finetuning of equivariance. I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks may help. Restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work may also help. This may lead to an interesting contribution to the field.

There are also a few minor issues. It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results. The angles on page 1 and page 5 are missing units. Are they degrees? On page three there is a sentence "In practice, it is difficult...". It is not M_g which is maximised or minimised. The loss over M_g is what gets maximised or minimised. Page 4 has footnote 2. You are just halving the activations. It is hard to call it a dropout. This constant factor can be passed to the following weights or the preceding weights. Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet? On page 7 there is Figure 3a and Figure 3b. In my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading. It is probably even incorrect. The distance between the same representations should be zero. This is also a way to verify that the experiments are performed correctly.
syntax_simple.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle. I am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. This is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks to my knowledge. The original papers only presented the concept. But see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear. Even those who are not very familiar with variational inference can understand it. Also the explanation of the IB principle is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising. The authors have done good work here.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference and information maximisation, p usually denotes the model. The symbol q represents the "inference engine". This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the underlying data distribution. They approximated it by the empirical distribution. Thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the predictive distribution in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) equals the integral of q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case. But this makes the two definitions contradict to each other! The notation should be consistent throughout the paper.

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training. They do this by tuning beta. However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE, the underlying model is different! In this case beta equals 1. For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z). This means r(z) is not a component in the model. While in VAE it is the prior distribution. It is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model. While in VAE that is the approximate posterior. It can be independently chosen. For example you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN. But p(z|x) can be a deep NN or a Gaussian process.

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision. The current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE. Please provide some intuitions if the VIB interpretation is preferred.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

Claim for independent work:
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016. That work is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive. Many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim. I commend the authors' honesty. But in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
syntax_simple.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach. The approach scores and ranks general-domain sentences. It uses a CNN classifier. The comparison to prior work is well done. Prior work used continuous or n-gram based language models. It is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection. One example is sum of difference of cross-entropies.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me. The paper argues that certain sections of a text or sentence are more important than others. A CNN achieves this. This is a strength of the paper. The paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ representation is more important. It also does not show why. The paper does not show if the combination of both representations matters more.

The textual description of the CNN is clear and detailed. The CNN uses one-hot or semi-supervised pre-trained embeddings. The description points out the important aspects. A picture of the layers would be worth a thousand words. The picture should show how inputs are combined.

The paper is overall well written. Some parentheses for citations are not necessary. One example is line 385. The authors should use citet versus citep properly.

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper. I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences. Line 443 describes this method. The method is based on a separate validation set. What validation data is used here? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. The paper does not discuss this. How sensitive are the models to this choice?

Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected. Figure 1 shows the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments follow. I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available. The experiment should not use just the development set. The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods. These examples would support the claims made in section 5.4.

Section 5.4 makes an argument about abstracting away from surface forms. Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod from 2015. Axelrod replaces some words with POS tags. This reduces LM data sparsity. A comparison would show whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this approach.

Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source and target Lewis-Moore LM data selection. That approach uses sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable. I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores. You could extend the CNN model to the bilingual or parallel setting. This extension might improve results.
syntax_simple.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
This submission pursues an interesting approach to character-based language modeling. The approach retains word-level representations in the context. It can also retain them in the output. However, the approach is not new. Kim et al. 2015 describes it. The submission cites this work. Jozefowicz et al. 2016 also describes it. Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission. They apply the approach using RNNs and LSTMs. Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion. They discuss different approaches to character-level modeling. I am missing such a discussion here. The authors should at least discuss this existing work. The remaining novelty of the approach would be its application to machine translation. It remains somewhat unclear how reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem. The translation-related part of the OOV problem should be elaborated here. Some of the claims of this submission seem somewhat exaggerated. Consider the statement in Section 2.3. It says the approach makes "the notion of vocabulary obsolete." The authors express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity without an explicit output vocabulary. Modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute. This is shown in arXiv:1609.08144.

Section 2.3 claims the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement is correct only if the units considered are limited to full word forms. Subwords can be used. Even individual characters can be used. Implicitly larger vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even infinite vocabularies can be covered. This requires a model different from the one proposed here. The corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Section 2.4 is not explicit enough. It is not explicit enough in my view.

The configuration of NCE is described in Section 3.4. It would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration. How did you arrive at your parameterization?

Section 4.1 discusses performance. Kim et al. 2015 came to similar conclusions. They evaluated the performance of using character embeddings at the output. You might want to mention this. You should discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein.

Section 4.2 discusses perplexity. There are ways to calculate perplexity for unknown words. There are ways to interpret it. See Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013.

Section 4.4 and Table 4 present results. The size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.

Minor comments follow. Page 2, bottom: "three different input layer" should be "three different input layers." Figure 1 has fonts that are way too small. Page 3, first item below Figure 1: "that we will note WE" should be "that we will denote WE." Section 2.3: "the parameters estimation" should be "the parameter estimation" or "the parameters' estimation." Page 5, first paragraph: "in factored way" should be "in a factored way." Page 5, second paragraph: "a n-best list, a nk-best list" should be "an n-best list, an nk-best list." Section 4.2, last sentence: "Despite adaptive gradient" is missing a verb and article.
syntax_simple.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward. Edward is a probabilistic programming language. It is built over TensorFlow and Python. It supports a broad range of most popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods. These methods appear in an easily usable form. The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques. These techniques are especially important from a representation learning perspective. The review is combined with two experiments. The first experiment implements various modern variational inference methods. The second experiment implements GPU-accelerated HMC.

The first experiment focuses on variational inference. It would be more valuable with a clear link to complete code. This code should reproduce the results provided. The HMC experiment looks OK. There is one exception. The paper characterises Stan as a hand-optimised implementation. This seems unfair. The code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific model. It is also not hand-optimised for this hardware configuration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your implementation. Please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist claims. I would suggest a different approach instead of current drama. You should compare head-to-head against Stan on single core. You should separately report the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation. You should also report speedups from GPU. These numbers would help the readers. Readers could estimate the performance of the method for other hardware configurations.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written. It is easy to read. The numerous code examples are helpful. They are also difficult. It is sometimes unclear what is missing. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide something. They should clearly link to a machine-readable companion. A Jupyter notebook would be great. Even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste from than a pdf. The paper is a pdf. The companion should have complete runnable code for all the examples.

Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic inference methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications. These publications are from the same group. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a). That paper covers a lot of similar material. It presents this material from a different perspective. It is unclear if the other paper has been published. It is unclear if it has been submitted somewhere. If so, where?

Significance:
It seems very likely Edward will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning. It will also impact deep learning.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction. This distinction is between specialised languages and Turing-complete languages. Stan is included among specialised languages. Edward is presented as Turing-complete. This seems unfair. I believe Stan is also Turing complete. Additionally no proof is provided. This proof should support the Turing-completeness of Edward.
syntax_simple.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
I want to point out something first. This paper is really long. It is 17 pages long. It has no supplementary material. ICLR does not have an official page limit. Authors should put themselves in the reviewer's shoes. They should not take undue advantage of this rule. Having 1 or 2 pages is ok. This is in addition to the conventional 8 page limit. More than doubling the pages is quite unfair.

Now I provide the review. The paper proposes a new artificial dataset. The dataset is for sequence learning. I call it artificial. It was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset. MNIST is a smallish dataset. It contains real images. The images show handwritten digits. The authors propose something in addition to the dataset. They propose to train recurrent networks. They use a schedule. The schedule goes over the length of the sequence. They call this "incremental learning". The experiments show something. Their proposed schedule is better than not having any schedule. This is true on this data set. They also show something else. Their proposed schedule is better than a few other intuitive schedules. The authors verify this. They do some ablation studies. The studies are over the model. They use the proposed dataset.

I have following issues with this paper.

I did not find anything novel in this paper. The proposed incremental learning schedule is nothing new. It is a natural thing to try. This is true when learning sequences. Similar ideas have already been tried. A number of authors tried them. These include Bengio 2015. These include Ranzato 2015. The only new piece of work is the ablation studies. The authors conduct these studies. They tease out something. They verify something. The improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used. This is indeed the case.

The authors only test their hypothesis on a single dataset. They propose this dataset. It is artificially generated. Why not use it on a real sequential dataset? Language modeling is such a dataset. Does the technique not work in that scenario? I am quite positive about something. This is for language modeling. The vocabulary size is huge there. The performance gains will be nowhere close to the 74%. The paper reports this 74%.

I am not convinced about the value. This value is of having this artificial dataset. Already there are so many real world sequential datasets available. These include datasets in text. These include datasets in speech. These include datasets in finance. These include datasets in other areas. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table? This is not super clear to me. Having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself. I almost felt something. This dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas work. It would have been so much better. The authors should have shown experiments on other datasets.

I said something already. The paper is way too long. A significant part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of experiments. These experiments
syntax_simple.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
Solar power is a miracle of modern science. There is one, tiny little problem, however. It's still more expensive than using other forms of power. The cost is the main issue. That goes for all forms of renewable energy. Renewable energy would be much better without this problem.

Many people will point out that installing solar power is on par with or even cheaper than building new power plants. These plants include nuclear or coal facilities. This is true in the very large scale. You're probably not going to build your own power plant. You don't have that expense to contend with. You need to look at the cost of a solar panel. You need to look at how much power it can produce on average. You should do the math. The numbers tell the story.

Some believe the government could invest some money. They think this investment could easily shut down one or two nuclear power plants. This view contains some false assumptions. Firstly, the government is subsidizing solar power purchases in California in a huge way. They are investing some money already. Secondly, the government does not operate the Nuclear Power Plants. Those are operated by private corporations. They are regulated by the government. The government provides oversight. Also, the primary cost of a nuclear power plant is the construction of the plant. The disposal of the nuclear material also costs money. The running of the plant itself does not cost as much. Shutting down a working plant would waste money. It would not save money.

I love solar power. I love it for all kinds of reasons. It's "point of use." This means there is very little loss due to long distance transmission. It's practically zero emissions. It's silent. That's a big thing for me. It provides the greatest benefit when the need is the highest. This happens in the summer. This happens in the daytime.

Possibly the best use of solar might be to run air conditioning. During the summer the sun is strong. The need for air is strong. You use the light provided by solar panels to help cool the building. Also, the panels sit on the roof. They provide shade for the building. Win/win.

Still, a pure cost benefit analysis tells a different story. It's still cheaper to use coal or natural gas to provide electricity.
syntax_simple.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad:
Say you're a merchant. You live in 17th century Amsterdam. There's a bunch of super-rich ladies there. They really, really love cumin. Cumin is a spice. Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam. You have to go to the middle east or India. You have to go there to get some of that fine stuff. That means it's super-expensive in Amsterdam. Over there, however, it grows like a weed. It costs very little money there. You could get some of that cheap cumin. You could bring it over to Amsterdam. You could make a lot of money doing this!

Unfortunately, there's only one way to do that. You have to send out a big-ass ship. The trip takes like nine months. That is HUGELY expensive. You have to get a ship. You have to get a captain and crew. They all want nine months worth of pay. The trip is also really risky. The boat could sink, after all. All the cumin could spoil as well.

So how do you accomplish this? You're not stupendously rich yourself. Very few people or groups are that rich. Maybe whole nations are that rich. So how do you finance this? You could go to a bank or money-lender. You could take out a loan there. The loan would have a very steep interest rate. That rate could almost eat up all of your profits. And what if the boat sank? You'd be completely bankrupt then. You'd be thrown into prison. Or maybe the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you come up with an idea. You can't finance this trip alone. But you could rather easily finance one tenth of the cost of the trip. You could do that fairly easily. And look at that. You have nine friends. All of them could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement. You decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip. You "buy stock" in the enterprise. Each person gets shares. Each share is worth one tenth of the total enterprise. You collect this money together. You pay for the boat and crew with it. You send them off. Then nine months later, it comes back. It has a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost. Each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits.

But what happens if your boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously. It's especially bad for the crew! But you only paid for one tenth of the cost. This was a cost you could afford to eat. You're not gonna get killed over it. The risk was spread around to 10 people. No one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit. One person didn't take an enormous hit.

Think about this example. Think about all the people involved in it. The fancy ladies got their cumin. They got it for cheaper than they would have otherwise. The shipwrights got work. They built a new ship. The captain and crew all got work. They got a salary. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, every single person is better off. It wouldn't have happened otherwise. This notion of "buying and selling stocks" had to exist for this to happen.

This is the advantage of a stock market. It moves capital around. Capital just lies around doing absolutely nothing in some places. The market moves it to where it can be put to use. In the meantime, everybody gets richer. It also distributes risk between lots of people. You don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems. The modern day American version of the stock market has problems. But the critique is this. It stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing. It is supposed to allocate capital. Capital should be put into productive use. The stock market stopped being a means to an end. It became an end unto itself. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea. You'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it. It is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones. We have cheap and plentiful food, medicine. We have all the other modern things we value so highly.

To be blunt, you probably won't be able to look at 2 similar wine bottles. You won't immediately figure out which one you'll like better. This is true unless you're very experienced with wines. What you can do is figure out what kind of wines you like in general. You have to actually try a few of those wines. This is how you figure out which wine types you like. Unfortunately, this can cost some money. Additionally, it's illegal to buy wine in the US if you're actually 5. Wines are generally divided by where the grapes were grown. They are also divided by the species of grape. The species is called the wine's "varietal."

Common Red Varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah (sometimes called Shiraz), Zinfandel

Common White Varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris (sometimes called Pinot Grigio), Riesling, Gewurztraminer

You should pay attention to what you like about wines. Do this when you taste wines. For example, many red wines have a distinctive taste. This taste makes your mouth feel dry. This is known as a "tannic" taste. It's caused by molecules called tannins. A tannic varietal might be good for you. This is true if you like tannic wines. Cabernet Sauvignon is a tannic varietal.

For white wines, common noticeable traits include acidity. They also include sugar content. Acidity means sourness. You probably don't need an explanation of what qualifies as sour. You probably don't need an explanation of what qualifies as sugary. Another common trait to look for is "oakiness." You can look for this in red wine. You can look for this in white wine. You might detect a wood-like scent in the wine. That means the wine has an "oaky" flavor.

Keep all this in mind. Remember that there's no such thing as a universally great wine. All that matters is which kind you like best. This is true even if that means choosing to drink a $10 jug of wine. You might choose this over a $500 bottle of fancy Cabernet from Bordeaux.

Also, ask the waiter when in doubt. Ask the sommelier. Ask the wine shop employee to help you out. You usually have a vague idea of what you want. They can help you find something you'd like. They can find something in your price range.

syntax_simple.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators. It identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. Machine learning techniques such as deep learning have achieved recent successes. More and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms. These algorithms detect attacks faster. However, these systems lack robustness. They struggle when facing previously unseen types of attacks. The number of new attacks is increasing. Many attacks target Internet of Things devices especially. Having a robust IDS becomes necessary. It must be able to spot unusual and new attacks. This work explores a possibility. We can leverage generative adversarial models. These models improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method. We name it SIGMA. It leverages adversarial examples. These examples strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. SIGMA uses Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics. SIGMA generates adversarial examples iteratively. It uses those examples to retrain a machine learning-based IDS. This continues until a convergence of the detection rate occurs. This means the detection system is not improving anymore. A round of improvement consists of three phases. First comes a generative phase. We use GANs and metaheuristics to generate instances in this phase. Second comes an evaluation phase. We calculate the detection rate of those newly generated attacks. Third comes a training phase. We train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method. We tested four standard machine learning classification algorithms. These algorithms act as IDS. We used a combination of GAN and a hybrid algorithm. This hybrid combines local-search and genetic algorithm. We generated new datasets of attacks. Our results show something important. SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks. It works against different machine learning based IDS. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS. We achieved improvements up to 100 percent. This happened after as little as two rounds of improvement.
syntax_simple.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs. They describe non-treelike evolutionary histories. They are a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes a collection of phylogenetic trees as input. It asks to construct a phylogenetic network. This network contains an embedding of each of the input trees. It has a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves. It runs in time O ( c k poly (n. Here k is the hybridization number of an optimal network. Also c is some positive constant. For the case of two trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before. An algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two trees had remained elusive prior to this article. The algorithm for two trees uses the close connection to acyclic agreement forests. This achieves a linear exponent in the running time. Previous algorithms for more than two trees relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying network topologies. They did this explicitly or implicitly. This leads to running times. These running times are not O ( c k poly (n for any c. The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two trees. So the reconstruction of the network poses major challenges. This is true even given the right agreement forest. We prove novel structural results. These results allow us to reconstruct a network. We do not have to guess the underlying topology. Our techniques generalize to more than three input trees. One key lemma is the exception. This lemma maps nodes in the network to tree nodes. Thus it minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem is to prove results. These results establish such a mapping for more than three trees. This is therefore the main open problem.
syntax_simple.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle. It is a simple subset-sum instance. It expresses that a natural number written in binary cannot be negative. We relate it to central problems in proof complexity. We relate it to central problems in algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds. These bounds apply to the Ideal Proof System. We call this system IPS. The bounds concern IPS refutation size of this instance. They are based on a well-known hypothesis. Shub and Smale stated this hypothesis. The hypothesis is about the hardness of computing factorials. IPS is the strong algebraic proof system. Grochow and Pitassi introduced it. Conversely, we show something else. Short IPS refutations of this instance bridge the gap. The gap is between sufficiently strong algebraic proof systems. The gap is between sufficiently strong semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS. They extend the paradigm. Forbes et al. introduced this paradigm. Lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained in that work. They used restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds. We demonstrate something important. The binary value principle captures the advantage. The advantage is of semi-algebraic reasoning over algebraic reasoning. This holds for sufficiently strong systems. Specifically, we show the following points. Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound. The lower bound applies to the size of IPS refutations. The refutations are of the binary value principle over the rationals. We define it as the unsatisfiable linear equation. The equation is i equals one to n, two to the power negative i plus one, times x sub i, minus one. The x sub i variables are boolean. Further, we consider the related conjecture. This conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound. The lower bound applies to the size of IPS refutations. These refutations are of a variant. The variant is of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems. Frege is such a system. Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation. It is not a direct translation of a boolean formula. Hence, similar to other results on algebraic proofs, IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds. They do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege. They do not necessarily entail lower bounds for its subsystems. Algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary. It is necessary for any algebraic proof system. The system must fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system. For strong enough algebraic proof systems it is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system. It simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems. It simulates most other known concrete propositional proof systems. We call it Cone Proof System. We abbreviate this as CPS. It serves as a semi-algebraic analogue. It is an analogue of the ideal proof system. CPS establishes the unsatisfiability. It establishes the unsatisfiability of collections. These collections contain polynomial equalities. These collections contain polynomial inequalities over the reals. It represents sum-of-squares proofs as algebraic circuits. It represents extensions as algebraic circuits. We prove something fundamental. IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS. This equivalence holds if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations. These refutations are of the binary value principle. This applies for the language of systems of equations. These systems have no zero-one solutions. This holds over both Z and Q.
syntax_simple.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper focuses on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application. It can also be applied in data mining and data manifold learning. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold. This makes the subsequent task much easier. The subsequent task could be clustering with k-means or any of its approximations. The approach reduces the dimensionality of data. However, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets. Two factors cause this problem. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. Second, one still has to operate with the same number of data points after the spectral embedding is complete. This may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means. The computational cost of these relaxations scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Also, they become prone to getting stuck in local minima. Their robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices. We call this the target subset. We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph. The representation preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. In particular, it allows one to ensure something important. Target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform such. This is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian. We call this ROM. The ROM approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace. It also allows one to exploit the conventional algorithms in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient. These conventional algorithms include approximations of k-means. This was verified in the numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real data. We also note something else. Our ROM approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way. This makes it the only feasible option for extremely large graphs. These graphs are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering. This applies in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, they may be used for quality control purposes. Third, they drastically reduce the problem size. This enables the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration. These sophisticated algorithms include more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm. We call this SDP. Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm to handle the full graph. The latter will be reported in a separate article.
syntax_simple.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We consider the problem of designing [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS). These codes must satisfy the (r , t) - Local Repair Property. Any t ( t) simultaneously failed nodes can be locally repaired. Each node is repaired with locality r . The parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers. They satisfy r k n and t - n k . We consider the functional repair model. We also use the sequential approach for repairing multiple failed nodes. Functional repair means something specific. The packet stored in each newcomer is not necessarily an exact copy of the lost data. It is a symbol. This symbol keeps the (r , t) -local repair property. The sequential approach means something specific too. The t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence. Each newcomer can be repaired from the live nodes. It can also be repaired from the newcomers ordered before it. We refer to such codes as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes (FLRC). These codes are the most general class of LRCs. They contain several subclasses of LRCs reported in the literature. In this paper, we aim to optimize the storage overhead. This is equivalently the code rate of FLRCs. We derive a lower bound on the code length n. This bound is given for t {2 , 3 } and any possible k , r . For t 2 , our bound generalizes the rate bound proved in earlier work. For t 3 , our bound improves the rate bound proved in earlier work. We also give some constructions of exact LRCs. These constructions are for t {2 , 3 }. Their length n achieves the bound of (n , k , r , t) -FLRC. This proves the tightness of our bounds. It also implies something important. There is no gap between the optimal code length of functional LRCs and exact LRCs. This holds for certain sets of parameters. Moreover, our constructions are over the binary field. They are of interest in practice for this reason.
syntax_simple.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a problem. A mobile agent constructs a map of its environment. The agent localizes itself within the map at the same time. Dense SLAM algorithms perform reconstruction. They perform localization at pixel granularity. These algorithms require a lot of computational power. This has hindered their use on low-power devices. These devices have constrained resources. Approximate computing can speed up SLAM implementations. The approximations must not prevent correct navigation. The agent must navigate correctly through the environment. Previous studies examined approximation in SLAM. They assumed something about the trajectory. The entire trajectory of the agent was known beforehand. The agent had not started yet. They focused on offline controllers. These controllers set approximation knobs at the start of the trajectory. The trajectory is usually not known ahead of time in practice. SLAMBooster is an application-aware control system. It operates online. It works for dense SLAM. It adaptively controls approximation knobs. This happens during the motion of the agent. SLAMBooster is based on a control technique. This technique is called proportional-integral-derivative controller. We call it PID controller. Our experiments showed something about this controller. This application-agnostic controller led to a reduction in localization accuracy. The reduction was unacceptable. SLAMBooster addresses this problem. It also exploits domain knowledge. This controls approximation. It performs smooth surface detection. It performs pose correction. We implemented SLAMBooster in the open-source SLAMBench framework. We evaluated it on more than a dozen trajectories. These trajectories came from the literature. They came from our own study too. Our experiments show results on the average. SLAMBooster reduces the computation time by 72 percent. It reduces energy consumption by 35 percent. This happens on an embedded platform. The accuracy of localization stays within reasonable bounds. These improvements make something feasible. SLAM can be deployed on a wider range of devices now.

A digital signature is a mathematical scheme. It verifies the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature gives a recipient very high confidence. The prerequisites must be satisfied. The message was created by a known sender. This is authenticity. The message was not altered in transit. This is integrity.

Digital signatures are a standard element. Most cryptographic protocol suites include them. They are commonly used for software distribution. They are used for financial transactions. They are used for contract management software. They are used in other cases. It is important to detect forgery or tampering in these cases.

They include the United States. They include Algeria. They include Turkey. They include India. They include Brazil. They include Indonesia. They include Mexico. They include Saudi Arabia. They include Uruguay. They include Switzerland. They include Chile. They include the countries of the European Union.

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography. They provide a layer of validation and security in many instances. Messages are sent through a non-secure channel. A digital signature is properly implemented. It gives the receiver reason to believe something. The message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respects. Properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Digital signature schemes are cryptographically based. This is the sense used here. They must be implemented properly. Then they are effective. They can also provide non-repudiation. The signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message. The signer also claims their private key remains secret. Some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature. The private key is exposed. The signature is still valid. Digitally signed messages may be anything representable as a bitstring. Examples include electronic mail. Examples include contracts. Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics. It develops methodologies and technologies. These enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers. The main benefit is searchability. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR). It is also known as computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training". Training is also called "enrollment". An individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice. It uses this analysis to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech. This results in increased accuracy. Systems exist that do not use training. These are called "speaker-independent" systems. Systems exist that use training. These are called "speaker dependent" systems.

Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces. Examples are voice dialing (e.g. "call home"). Other examples are call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"). Applications also include domotic appliance control. They include search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken). Simple data entry is another application (e.g., entering a credit card number). Preparation of structured documents is included (e.g. a radiology report). Other applications are determining speaker characteristics. Speech-to-text processing is an application (e.g., word processors or emails). Aircraft systems use it (usually termed direct voice input).

The term voice recognition refers to identifying the speaker. The term speaker identification also refers to this. It identifies the speaker rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech. This applies in systems trained on a specific person's voice. It can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker. This happens as part of a security process.

Speech recognition has a long history from the technology perspective. It has seen several waves of major innovations. Most recently, the field has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances are evidenced by the surge of academic papers published in the field. More importantly, they are evidenced by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.

Control theory is a field of mathematics. It deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm. This model governs the application of system inputs. The inputs drive the system to a desired state. The process minimizes any delay. It minimizes overshoot. It minimizes steady-state error. It ensures a level of control stability. The aim is often to achieve a degree of optimality.

A controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required to do this. This controller monitors the controlled process variable. People call this the PV. The controller compares it with the reference or set point. People call this the SP. The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable is called the error signal. People also call it the SP-PV error. This error is applied as feedback. The feedback generates a control action. The action brings the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects are also studied. These aspects are controllability and observability. Control theory is used in control system engineering. It designs automation. This automation has revolutionized manufacturing. It has revolutionized aircraft. It has revolutionized communications and other industries. It has created new fields. Robotics is one such field.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style. This style is known as the block diagram. The transfer function appears in it. People also know this as the system function or network function. It is a mathematical model. This model represents the relation between the input and output. It is based on the differential equations. These equations describe the system.

Control theory dates from the 19th century. The theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described then. James Clerk Maxwell first described it. Edward Routh further advanced control theory in 1874. Charles Sturm also advanced it. Adolf Hurwitz advanced it in 1895. They all contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria. Nicolas Minorsky developed PID control theory from 1922 onwards.

Mathematical control theory has a major application in control systems engineering. This field deals with the design of process control systems for industry. Other applications range far beyond this. Control theory is the general theory of feedback systems. It is useful wherever feedback occurs. Control theory has applications in life sciences. It has applications in computer engineering. It has applications in sociology and operations research.

Data dredging is also known as data snooping or p-hacking. It is the misuse of data analysis. Researchers use it to find patterns in data. They can present these patterns as statistically significant. This dramatically increases the risk of false positives. It also understates this risk. Researchers do this by performing many statistical tests on the data. They only report those tests. These are the tests that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses. Researchers use a single data set. They do this by exhaustively searching the data. They might search for combinations of variables. These variables might show a correlation. They might search for groups of cases or observations. These groups show differences in their mean. They might show differences in their breakdown by some other variable.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on probability. This is the probability that a particular result would arise. Chance alone would be at work. These tests necessarily accept some risk. This is the risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type. These are mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis. This level of risk is called the significance. Researchers perform large numbers of tests. Some produce false results of this type. Hence 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level. This is erroneous. Another 1% might be reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level. This is also erroneous. This happens by chance alone. Researchers test enough hypotheses. It is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant. This is misleading. Almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain some spurious correlations. These are examples. Researchers use data mining techniques. They are not cautious. These results can easily mislead them.

Data dredging is an example. It disregards the multiple comparisons problem. One form exists. Subgroups are compared. Researchers do not alert the reader. They omit the total number of subgroup comparisons examined.

Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) is a private research university in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Andrew Carnegie established one of its predecessors in 1900. He called it the Carnegie Technical Schools. It became the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1912. It began granting four-year degrees in the same year. The Carnegie Institute of Technology merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research in 1967. Andrew Mellon and Richard B. Mellon founded that institute in 1913. It was formerly a part of the University of Pittsburgh.[10] Carnegie Mellon University has operated as a single institution since the merger.

The university consists of seven colleges and independent schools. These are the College of Engineering, College of Fine Arts, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Tepper School of Business, Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, and the School of Computer Science.[11][12] The university has its main campus. The campus is located 5 miles (8 km) from Downtown Pittsburgh. It also has over a dozen degree-granting locations in six continents. These include degree-granting campuses in Qatar, Silicon Valley, and Kigali, Rwanda (Carnegie Mellon University Africa). It has partnerships with universities across the United States. It also partners with universities in the United Kingdom, Portugal, Japan, China, Mexico, and Italy.[13]

Carnegie Mellon is known for its advances in research and new fields of study. It is notably home to many firsts in computer science. These include the first computer science, machine learning, and robotics departments. It pioneered the field of management science.[14] It was home to the first drama program in the United States. CMU is classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very High Research Activity".[15] The university had research and development expenditures of $386 million in 2020.[16] Past and present faculty and alumni include 20 Nobel Prize laureates, 13 Turing Award winners, 26 members of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 39 fellows of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, 91 members of the National Academies, 142 Emmy Award winners, 52 Tony Award laureates, and 12 Academy Award winners.[17] Carnegie Mellon enrolls 15,818 students across its multiple campuses. These students come from 117 countries. The university employs more than 1,400 faculty members. It has an active alumni base of over 112,000.[18]

Matt Wozniak was born on January 6, 1983. He is a Canadian curler. He comes from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team. That team curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink in 2005. The rink included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. The 2006-07 season arrived. Richter and Melnuk left the team. They were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team disbanded after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. They played their first season together. They were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship. This was Manitoba's provincial championship. Their first Grand Slam event as a team came at the end of the season. It was at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two games. Then they were eliminated.

The 2008-09 season concluded. The McEwen team was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. They had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs. They finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

The 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier took place. The McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans. Those were the Jason Gunnlaugson team. This happened in the semi-finals. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final. They had been the favourite in that particular matchup vs Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's rink made it to his first provincial final in 2010. He lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial final. The game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba. The Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach. They were treated very much as the home team. They were crowd favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 season off well. They defeated provincial rival Jeff Stoughton. They won the World Cup of Curling. This was his first ever Grand Slam title. It happened in November, 2010. The team had a runner-up result in the provincial finals of 2010. The team also had 4 victories. They were leading the overall money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010. The McEwen team was named as a nominee for the provincial team of the year. This was by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The team continued their strong season that year. They defeated provincial rival Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard team in the extra end of the final. They won their second career Grand Slam. This was their second of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial. They were the top seed this time. They were also ranked 1st in Canada. They once again lost to Stoughton in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship. They lost by one point in the final end. The McEwen team then lost their third straight provincial final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship. This time they lost to Rob Fowler. This tied a provincial record for consecutive final losses. The record was previously set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was avoided in 2013. The McEwen rink failed to reach the final. They again lost to the rival Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again at the 2014 Safeway Championship the team lost the final to Stoughton.

Wozniak was ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list. He lost his fifth provincial final in six years in 2015. He lost to Reid Carruthers.

Wozniak's rink won their first provincial title in 2016. This sent them to their first Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships. Modern Greek art is art from a specific period. This period stretches between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century.

These islands were under other European powers' rule. Thus they were able to assimilate the radical artistic changes better. These changes were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th century.
