This paper, serving as an extension of the Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, demonstrates that CNN representations at the FC7 layer are, to a certain extent, equivariant to various classes of transformations and establishes that training with a certain group of transformations makes the representations more equivalent.

The authors, having performed a large amount of experiments involving the training of over 30 networks with different forms of jitter, present work that is quite impressive in scope. However, finding a main message within this work proves rather difficult. While the authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15 study, it remains hard to identify novel insights beyond the already known fact that jitter helps to achieve invariance. Although the evaluation appears to be mostly correct, the paper does not seem to be solving the task that is advertised in its title particularly well.

Major issues, which are found in the experiments with the representation distances, include the following points. The selection of only FC7 appears somewhat controversial, given that it is followed merely by a single classification layer, FC8, leading to the common output of class likelihoods. Since FC8 constitutes just a linear projection, what the equivalence map accomplishes is simply to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Performing similar experiments on additional layers would probably prove more useful, especially considering that the networks are already trained. The experiment involving representation distance is missing information about what the classification error on the testing dataset actually is, which would answer the question of whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all. Regarding the experiment with K-NN, it remains unclear whether this measurement is performed per each test set example or after training the equivalence map. More clarity would be achieved by demonstrating that networks trained on similar groups of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task. The proposed method does not appear to improve equivariance consistently across all tasks. Especially given that λ₁ and λ₂ have such small values, the loss becomes basically equal to simple data jitter since it merely adds up the loss of the original and transformed images. Perhaps the issue lies in the selection of the FC7 layer itself.

In general, while this paper shows some interesting results concerning FC7 equivariance, it does not appear to be drawing many interesting new observations from these experiments. Due to various issues with the equivalence experiments and the finetuning of equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work may potentially lead to an interesting contribution to the field.

Several minor issues also warrant attention. The new criterion for equivariance mapping has not been experimentally verified to help gain better results. The angles referenced on pages 1 and 5 are missing units, presumably degrees. On page three, where it states "In practice, it is difficult...", what is actually maximised or minimised is not M_g itself but rather the loss over M_g. Regarding page 4, footnote 2, if one is merely halving the activations, calling it dropout becomes difficult since this constant factor can be passed to the following or preceding weights. Whether the network used for RVL-CDIP shares the same architecture as Alexnet remains unspecified. On page 7, in Figures 3a and 3b, turning the diagonal elements to white appears, in my opinion, really misleading and probably even incorrect, considering that the distance between identical representations should be zero, which also provides a method for verifying that the experiments are performed correctly.
syntax_complex.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks, since the original papers only presented the concept, but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference, and the explanation of the IB principle, which provides the theoretical foundation for the approach, is equally clear. The experimental results, which demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method across multiple domains, seem to be very promising and suggest practical utility.

I found the presentation for the model, particularly regarding the notation and the relationships between different probability distributions, a bit confusing. In variational inference and information maximisation approaches, p usually denotes the model while q represents the "inference engine", which means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution**, being approximated by the empirical distribution, thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3, which raises the question: predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this interpretation makes the two definitions contradict to each other, creating confusion about the actual structure!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training, achieved by tuning beta. However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE, which occurs in this case when beta equals 1, the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z), which means r(z) is not a component in the model, while in VAE it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model as a fundamental component, while in VAE that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen, meaning you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process.

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure, including the mathematical notation and the relationships between components, is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE while providing some intuitions if the VIB interpretation is preferred.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive, with many people publishing the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty, but in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
syntax_complex.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier, where comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear whether the paper also compared against bilingual data selection, such as the sum of difference of cross-entropies.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text or sentence are more important than others and that this is achieved by employing a CNN architecture. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ representation, or indeed the combination of both representations, is more important and why this might be the case.

The textual description of the CNN, whether using one-hot encoding or semi-supervised learning using pre-trained embeddings, is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects that readers need to understand. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words in clarifying the architecture.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary, with \citet being preferable to \citep in certain contexts, as seen in line 385.

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences, as described in line 443, which is based on a separate validation set, raising several questions. What validation data is used here, and how exactly is it selected? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen, nor how sensitive the models are to variations in this selection process. Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected, though Figure 1 shows that the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments that merit consideration include the following. I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set that was used. The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4, which would strengthen the argument considerably. In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4, another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this approach.

Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source and target Lewis-Moore LM data selection, particularly the sum of difference of cross-entropies, meaning that a reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the bilingual or parallel setting.
syntax_complex.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output, though the approach itself is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016), both of whom already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also noteworthy is that Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work that already establishes important precedents. The remaining novelty of the approach then would be its application to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem, given that the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be elaborated here with greater specificity. That said, some of the claims of this submission seem somewhat exaggerated, like the statement made in Sec. 2.3 about "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity without an explicit output vocabulary, and modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144.

Concerning Sec. 2.3, you claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary, which is a statement that only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms, since using subwords and even individual characters means that implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion, even though this requires a model different from the one proposed here, suggesting that the corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified, as the description provided in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view to understand the complete methodology. Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4, which would help readers reproduce the work. In Sec. 4.1, you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions with respect to the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein, which remain relevant. Regarding Sec. 4.2, there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013), which should be acknowledged.

In Sec. 4.4 and Table 4, the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here for completeness.

Minor comments include: p. 2, bottom: three different input layer should be three different input layers (plural); Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small; p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE should be that we will denote WE; Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation should be the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation); p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way should be in a factored way; p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list should be an n-best list, an nk-best list; Sec. 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient requires a verb and article.
syntax_complex.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward, which is a probabilistic programming language that has been built over TensorFlow and Python, and which supports a broad range of the most popular contemporary methods that currently exist in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward library provides what can be considered an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in a form that is easily usable. The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques, especially when viewed from a representation learning perspective, which is combined with two experiments focusing on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC. The first experiment, which concerns variational inference, would be more valuable if there was a clear link provided to complete code that could reproduce the results that have been provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except that characterising Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair given that the code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific model and hardware configuration under consideration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your implementation, so please do not ruin the picture that you have presented by making unsubstantiated sensationalist claims. Instead of the current drama that is present, I would suggest comparing head-to-head against Stan on single core while separately reporting the extra speedups that you gain from parallelisation and GPU, which are separate considerations. These numbers would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method when applied to other hardware configurations that they might be using.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read for the intended audience. The numerous code examples are helpful, but also difficult in that it is sometimes unclear what elements are missing from them. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion, where a Jupyter notebook would be great, but even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper, with complete runnable code that covers all the examples that have been presented.

Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic inference methods that has been assembled. In terms of the paper itself, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications of the same group that have already appeared. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a), which covers a lot of similar material, although it does so from a different perspective. It is unclear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where that publication venue is.

Significance:
It seems very likely that Edward will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning going forward.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages, which include Stan, and Turing-complete languages such as Edward, which seems unfair as I believe Stan is also Turing complete, and additionally no proof is provided to support the claimed Turing-completeness of Edward.
syntax_complex.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
First up, I want to point out that this paper, which runs to some 17 pages without any supplementary material whatsoever, is really long. While ICLR does not have an official page limit that authors must adhere to, it would be nice if authors, putting themselves in the reviewer's shoes and considering the workload involved, did not take undue advantage of this rule that permits unlimited length. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the conventional 8 page limit that most venues impose is ok, but more than doubling the pages, as has been done here, is quite unfair to those tasked with reviewing.

Now for the review: The paper proposes a new artificial dataset for sequence learning, which I call artificial because it was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset, itself a smallish dataset of real images of handwritten digits that has been widely used in the community. In addition to the dataset that they introduce, the authors propose to train recurrent networks using a schedule over the length of the sequence, an approach which they call "incremental learning" throughout their exposition. The experiments that they present show that their proposed schedule, when applied to this particular data set, is better than not having any schedule at all. Furthermore, they also show through additional experiments that their proposed schedule is better than a few other intuitive schedules that one might naturally consider. The authors verify this claim by doing some ablation studies over the model architecture on the proposed dataset that they have created.

I have the following issues with this paper that prevent me from recommending acceptance:

-- I did not find anything novel in this paper that would warrant publication. The proposed incremental learning schedule, which forms the core contribution, is nothing new and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences of varying lengths. Similar ideas have already been tried by a number of authors working in this area, including Bengio 2015 and Ranzato 2015, who explored curriculum learning. The only new piece of work that I can identify is the ablation studies which the authors conduct to tease out and verify that indeed the improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used rather than other factors.

-- Furthermore, the authors only test their hypothesis on a single dataset which they themselves propose and which is artificially generated rather than drawn from real applications. Why not use it on a real sequential dataset, such as language modeling, which would be more convincing? Does the technique not work in that scenario, and if not, why? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling, where the vocabulary size is huge and the sequences are naturally occurring, the performance gains will be nowhere close to the 74% that is reported in the paper.

-- I'm not convinced about the value of having this artificial dataset added to the community's resources. Already there are so many real world sequential datasets available, including datasets in text, speech, finance and other areas that could benefit from such techniques. What exactly this dataset brings to the table is not super clear to me given these alternatives. While having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas work rather than addressing a genuine need.

-- As I said earlier, the paper is way too long for the contributions it makes. A significant part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of experiments which are completely unrelated to the main message that the paper attempts to convey. For instance, the experiment presented in Section 6.2 is completely unrelated to the story of the paper and could be removed. Same is true with the transfer learning experiments of Section 6.4, which seem tangential at best.

Solar power, being a miracle of modern science, has one tiny little problem that cannot be ignored: it's still more expensive than using other forms of power. If it wasn't for the cost, which remains a significant barrier, it would be a much better idea, though that observation applies equally to all forms of renewable energy that we might consider implementing.

Many people will point out that installing solar power, when undertaken at sufficient scale, is on par with or even cheaper than building new power plants such as nuclear or coal facilities. While this is true in the very large scale, which involves industrial implementation, you're probably not going to build your own power plant and therefore don't have that enormous expense to contend with in your personal calculations. Look at the cost of a solar panel versus how much power *on average* it can produce over time, then do the math carefully.

> I believe if the government invested some money they could easily shut down one or two nuclear power plants

You seem to be laboring under some false assumptions that need correcting. Firstly, the government is subsidizing solar power purchases in California in a huge way, meaning they *are* investing some money already. Secondly, the government does not operate the Nuclear Power Plants, which are operated by private corporations that answer to shareholders. They are merely *regulated* by the government through oversight agencies. Also, the primary cost of a nuclear power plant, which is substantial, is the construction of the plant and the disposal of the nuclear material rather than the running of the plant itself. Shutting down a working plant would waste money rather than save money.

Like I said, I love solar power for all kinds of reasons that appeal to me. It's "point of use," which means there is very little loss due to long distance transmission that plagues centralized generation. It's practically zero emissions. It's silent, which is a big thing for me personally. It provides the greatest benefit when the need is the highest, occurring in the summer during the daytime hours.

Possibly the best use of solar might be to run air conditioning, since during the summer when the sun is strong, the need for air conditioning is equally strong. Use the light provided by solar panels, which capture abundant energy, to help cool the building while the panels on the roof provide shade. Win/win.

Still, on a pure cost-benefit analysis, it's cheaper to use coal or natural gas.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice), expressing their desire for it constantly. Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, requiring you to travel to the middle east or India to get some of that fine stuff, which makes it *super-expensive* in your local market. Over there, however, it grows like a weed, costing very little money to acquire. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, transporting it across vast distances, you could make a lot of money from the price differential!

Unfortunately, the only way to accomplish that is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months, embarking on a lengthy and arduous journey. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all want nine months worth of pay, demanding compensation for their time), but it is also really risky, given all the dangers that lurk along the route. The boat could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil during the voyage.

So how do you accomplish this undertaking? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich, possessing such massive resources), how do you finance this risky venture? You could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your profits, leaving you with virtually nothing. And what if the boat sank beneath the waves? You'd be completely bankrupt, facing financial ruin, and be thrown into prison, assuming the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first, exacting revenge for the unpaid debt.

So, you come up with an idea, devising an ingenious solution. You can't finance this trip alone, lacking sufficient capital. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip, contributing a manageable portion. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip, possessing similar means. So you all come to an agreement, negotiating terms: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise, acquiring ownership), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise that you're launching together. With this money, pooling your resources, you pay for the boat and crew, send them off on their journey, and then nine months later, after waiting anxiously, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin that commands premium prices. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, exceeding all expectations, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits generated by the successful voyage.

But what happens if your boat sinks beneath the ocean waves? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew, who lose their lives!), but you only paid for one tenth of the cost, having limited your exposure, and this was a cost you could afford to eat, absorbing the loss without catastrophic consequences, meaning you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, distributing the burden, no one landed in debtors prison, avoiding total ruin. Everyone took a small hit, suffering a manageable loss, instead of one person taking an enormous hit that would destroy them financially.

Think about this example, considering its implications, and all the people involved in it, benefiting from the transaction. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise, paying less). The shipwrights got work building a new ship, earning their wages. The captain and crew all got work and a salary, supporting their families. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin, expanding his business. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process, achieving prosperity. In short, *every single person is better off*, improving their circumstances, and it wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stocks" didn't exist, enabling such ventures.

This is the advantage of a stock market, demonstrating its value. It moves capital around from where it just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use, creating wealth, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer through these productive investments. It also distributes risk between lots of people, spreading exposure, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time, living in constant fear.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions, operating in its current form. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use, serving the real economy) and stopped being a means to an end, becoming disconnected, and it became an end unto itself, existing for its own sake. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea, enabling commerce, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it on principle. It is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly, enjoying their benefits daily.

Since the energy of the clap remains unchanged, we need to look at where that energy is going. In a regular clap occurring on earth, the energy of the collision goes into a variety of things, which include:

1) sound 

2) deformation of your hands

3) heat

4) some others that are probably constant in both scenarios and I won't address

Let's model, albeit horribly roughly, a clap consisting of 2 hands, each at 500g moving at 2m/s, which gives us E=mv2 so E= 4J roughly. 

Even though a clap would be considered an ellastic collision, there is likely some small energy loss to deformation, and I would expect to see some damage to cells under a microscope but very little. The biggest consumer of energy is going to be the heat given off. From [here](_URL_0_), which provides timing data, we see a clap is about 20ms long (super rough) and from [here](_URL_1_) we can see the sound power of a few similar things, which allows us to say an alarm clock is close enough. Even if we're wrong by a factor of a 100x, it's still close enough for this discussion that we're having. By doing the roughest, dirtiest integration of the sound wave shown in the first link with the power output of the table in the second, we get a total energy of 2x10^-6 J of energy from a clap. Compared to the 4J of input energy into the collision occurring on earth, the sound energy is only 0.00005% of the total released. The rest, constituting the overwhelming majority, goes to heat and deformation, and I wouldn't even bother guessing at what the ratio is between those two components. 

So, to answer your question that was posed: 

On earth, only 0.00005% of the energy goes into the sound of a clap, while the rest goes into heat and deformation of your hands. In space, where no medium exists for sound propagation, 0% of the energy goes into sound and that tiny bit that would have gone into sound on earth simply goes into more heat instead. The energy of the sound of the clap is so low by comparison to the heat given off by the collision to start with that the interaction is essentially unchanged except you hear no sound whatsoever.

To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with wines, you probably won't be able to look at two similar wine bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better, even after examining them carefully. What you can do, however, is figure out what kind of wines you like in general, which requires a systematic approach. To figure out which wine types you prefer, you have to actually try a few of those wines, sampling them thoughtfully and paying close attention to their characteristics. Unfortunately, this exploration can cost some money, especially if you're seeking quality examples. Additionally, if you're actually five years old, then it's illegal to buy wine in the US, making this entire endeavor impossible for young children.

Wines are generally divided by where the grapes were grown and the species of grape, which is called the wine's "varietal," a classification system that helps organize the vast world of wine. Common Red Varietals include Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah (sometimes called Shiraz, depending on the region), and Zinfandel. Common White Varietals include Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris (sometimes called Pinot Grigio when produced in Italy), Riesling, and Gewurztraminer.

When you taste wines, pay attention to what you like about them, noting the specific qualities that appeal to your palate. For example, many red wines have a distinctive taste that makes your mouth feel dry, which is known as a "tannic" taste because it's caused by molecules called tannins that naturally occur in grape skins. If you like tannic wines, discovering that preference early on, a tannic varietal like Cabernet Sauvignon might be particularly good for you. For white wines, common noticeable traits include acidity, which manifests as sourness, and sugar content, both of which significantly affect the overall flavor profile. You probably don't need an explanation of what qualifies as sour or sugary, since these are familiar sensations. Another common trait to look for in red or white wine is "oakiness," a quality that emerges during barrel aging. If you detect a wood-like scent in the wine, that means the wine has an "oaky" flavor, resulting from contact with oak barrels during fermentation or aging.

With all this in mind, remember that there's no such thing as a universally great wine that everyone will appreciate equally. All that matters is which kind you like best, even if that means choosing to drink a ten-dollar jug of wine over a five-hundred-dollar bottle of fancy Cabernet from Bordeaux. Also, when in doubt, ask the waiter, sommelier, or wine shop employee to help you out, since they possess expertise. Usually if you have a vague idea of what you want, they can help you find something you'd like in your price range.

syntax_complex.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: When you transmit at high speed, you can't think of the signals as digital in a wire, which means you have to think of the signal as an analog signal instead. Signals don't change instantly from 1 to 0, and they take time to travel in a cable, which is an important consideration. A signal in a cat 5 cable travels at 0.64 times the speed of light, or 4.8 to 5.3 ns per meter, which becomes significant when dealing with 100Mbit ethernet. So 100 * 10^6 bits per second equals 100 bits in 1000 ns, which means 1 bit in 10 ns. Therefore, if the ethernet cable is longer than 2 meters, there are more than one bit in the cable at any given time. Since a cable can be 100 m long, there will be 50 bits in the cable simultaneously, making it obvious that the signal is not the same throughout the entire cable. The bitrate in the cable is in practice higher because of encoding schemes that are used. This is an image of how a 100Mbit ethernet signal looks like in practice: URL_1. Here you have an eye diagram where you overlap different signals to see the pattern: URL_0. The way to look at this is that the system has to determine whether the signal is at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom where the black gaps are located. You can see that it is noisy and the holes, which are called eyes, are quite small in size. The smaller the eyes are, the harder it is to determine where the signal is, and if they disappear completely, you can't detect the signal anymore. So now when you see that the signal is noisy and analog rather than digital, you are starting to realize that you need cables that behave in certain ways to maintain signal integrity. How a signal propagates depends on the distance between the wires and the thickness and other material along the wire, as well as being affected by other factors. There will be interference from the surrounding environment and the other wire pairs, which is why the wire has to be twisted at different rates relative to each other to minimize interference between them. So to have a wire with known parameters that works with the hardware, you have to have standards that everyone follows. You can run the signal over other wires if you know what you are doing and understand the principles. If the wires in the pairs would have not been parallel or the pairs had been closer together, it would have not worked properly for signal transmission.

syntax_complex.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS), which identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks, serves as a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms that detect attacks faster. However, these systems, lacking robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks, present significant limitations. With the increasing number of new attacks, especially those targeting Internet of Things devices, having a robust IDS that is able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, which leverages adversarial examples to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial examples iteratively, using them to retrain a machine learning-based IDS until a convergence of the detection rate occurs, meaning the detection system is not improving anymore. A round of improvement consists of a generative phase, in which we use GANs and metaheuristics to generate instances; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks that have been generated. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS, employing a combination of GAN and a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm to generate new datasets of attacks. Our results demonstrate that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS to up to 100 after completing as little as two rounds of improvement.
syntax_complex.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks, which are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories, thus constitute a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network, defined as the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one, serves as a key measure of network complexity. The Hybridization Number problem, taking as input a collection of phylogenetic trees, asks to construct a phylogenetic network that contains an embedding of each of the input trees while having a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, running in time O ( c k poly (n, with k being the hybridization number of an optimal network and c some positive constant. For the case of two trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before, whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two trees had, prior to this article, remained elusive. The algorithm for two trees, using the close connection to acyclic agreement forests, achieves a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two trees, either explicitly or implicitly relying on a brute force search through all possible underlying network topologies, led to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n for any c. The connection to acyclic agreement forests being much weaker for more than two trees, even given the right agreement forest, the reconstruction of the network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results that allow us to reconstruct a network without having to guess the underlying topology. Our techniques, generalizing to more than three input trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the network to tree nodes and thus minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network, demonstrate broad applicability. The main open problem therefore is to prove results establishing such a mapping for more than three trees, which would complete the generalization of our approach.
syntax_complex.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle, which constitutes a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary cannot be negative, relating it to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of this instance, basing them on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system that was introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of this instance bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results, extending to full-fledged IPS the paradigm that was introduced in Forbes et al., whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning for sufficiently strong systems. Specifically, we show the following: Conditional IPS lower bounds: item Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals, defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation i 1 n 2 - i 1 x i - 1 for boolean x i 's. Further, the related -conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS or for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege. 1 1 footnote 1 Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula, hence, similar to and other results on algebraic proofs (e.g., Razborov), IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems. Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: item Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems it is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems (and most other known concrete propositional proof systems) under the name Cone Proof System (CPS), serving as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals by representing sum-of-squares proofs (and extensions) as algebraic circuits. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS iff IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle (for the language of systems of equations that have no 01-solutions) over both Z and Q.
syntax_complex.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians, along with their spectral embeddings, play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper, while focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application, can also be applied in data mining, data manifold learning, and related domains. Spectral embedding, by providing a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold, makes the subsequent task—whether clustering with k-means or any of its approximations—much easier to accomplish. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets, which can be attributed to two factors that compound the difficulty. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace, making the initial phase computationally demanding. Second, even after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points, a circumstance which may ruin the efficiency of the approach entirely. For example, clustering of the embedded data, which is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means, has computational cost that scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Also, these methods become prone to getting stuck in local minima, meaning their robustness depends critically on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices, which we designate as the target subset. We develop two novel algorithms for achieving such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. In particular, our approach allows one to ensure that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform such an analysis. That consistency is achieved by constructing a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset, which reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace, allows us to exploit the conventional algorithms—such as approximations of k-means—in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient. This advantage was verified in the numerical clustering experiments conducted with both synthetic and real data. We also note that our ROM approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, making it the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our algorithms, each addressing different practical needs. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, they may be used for quality control purposes. Third, because they drastically reduce the problem size, they enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration, including more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming (SDP) instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm. Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm designed to handle the full graph, which will be reported in a separate article.
syntax_complex.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We consider the problem of designing [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS) that satisfy the (r , t) - Local Repair Property , where any t ( t) simultaneously failed nodes can be locally repaired, each with locality r , the parameters n , k , r , t being positive integers such that r k n and t - n k . We consider both the functional repair model and the sequential approach for repairing multiple failed nodes, where by functional repair we mean that the packet stored in each newcomer is not necessarily an exact copy of the lost data but rather a symbol that keeps the (r , t) -local repair property, and by the sequential approach we mean that the t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence such that each newcomer can be repaired from the live nodes together with the newcomers that are ordered before it. Such codes, which we refer to as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes (FLRC), represent the most general class of LRCs and contain several subclasses of LRCs that have been reported in the literature. In this paper, we aim to optimize the storage overhead, which is equivalently the code rate, of FLRCs. We derive a lower bound on the code length n given t {2 , 3 } and any possible k , r , where for t 2 our bound generalizes the rate bound that was proved in , while for t 3 our bound improves the rate bound that was proved in . We also give some constructions of exact LRCs for t {2 , 3 } whose length n achieves the bound of (n , k , r , t) -FLRC, which proves the tightness of our bounds and also implies that there is no gap between the optimal code length of functional LRCs and exact LRCs for certain sets of parameters. Moreover, our constructions, being over the binary field, are of considerable interest in practice due to their practical implementability and computational efficiency in real-world distributed storage applications.
syntax_complex.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is the problem of constructing a map of a mobile agent's environment while simultaneously localizing the agent within that map. Dense SLAM algorithms, which perform reconstruction and localization at pixel granularity, require substantial computational power, a requirement that has hindered their use on low-power resource-constrained devices. Approximate computing can be used to speed up SLAM implementations, provided that the approximations introduced do not prevent the agent from navigating correctly through the environment. Previous studies examining approximation in SLAM have assumed that the entire trajectory of the agent is known before the agent starts, focusing on offline controllers that set approximation knobs at the start of the trajectory. In practice, however, the trajectory is usually not known ahead of time, and allowing knob settings to change dynamically opens up more opportunities for reducing both computation time and energy consumption. In this paper, we describe SLAMBooster, an application-aware, online control system for dense SLAM that adaptively controls approximation knobs during the motion of the agent. Although SLAMBooster is based on a control technique called proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, our experiments showed that this application-agnostic controller led to an unacceptable reduction in localization accuracy. To address this problem, SLAMBooster also exploits domain knowledge for controlling approximation by performing smooth surface detection and pose correction. Having implemented SLAMBooster in the open-source SLAMBench framework, we evaluated it on more than a dozen trajectories drawn from both the literature and our own study. Our experiments show that on average, SLAMBooster reduces the computation time by 72 percent and energy consumption by 35 percent on an embedded platform, while maintaining the accuracy of localization within reasonable bounds, improvements that make it feasible to deploy SLAM on a wider range of devices.
syntax_complex.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: While the Commission has a monopoly on initiating legislation, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union, exercising their authority during the legislative process, have powers of amendment and veto. According to articles 9 and 10 of the Treaty on European Union, the EU observes "the principle of equality of its citizens," being meant to be founded on "representative democracy." In practice, equality and democracy are deficient because the elected representatives in the Parliament, unable to act against the Commission's wishes, cannot initiate legislation, because citizens of smallest countries have ten times the voting weight in Parliament as citizens of the largest countries, and because "qualified majorities" or consensus of the Council are required to legislate. The justification for this "democratic deficit" under the Treaties is usually thought to be that completion integration of the European economy and political institutions required the technical coordination of experts, while popular understanding of the EU developed and nationalist sentiments, remaining strong in the post-war period, gradually declined. Over time, this has meant the Parliament gradually assumed more voice: from being an unelected assembly, to its first direct elections occurring in 1979, to having increasingly more rights in the legislative process. Citizens' rights are therefore limited compared to the democratic polities existing within all European member states: under TEU article 11 citizens and associations have the rights such as publicising their views and submitting an initiative that must be considered by the Commission with one million signatures. TFEU article 227 contains a further right for citizens to petition the Parliament on issues which affect them. Parliament elections, taking place every five years, require that votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote. There are 750 MEPs and their numbers are "degressively proportional" according to member state size. This means that—although the Council is meant to be the body representing member states—in the Parliament citizens of smaller member states have more voice than citizens in larger member states. MEPs divide, as they do in national Parliaments, along political party lines: the conservative European People's Party is currently the largest, and the Party of European Socialists leads the opposition. Parties do not receive public funds from the EU, as the Court of Justice held in Parti ecologiste "Les Verts" v Parliament that this was entirely an issue to be regulated by the member states. The Parliament's powers include calling inquiries into maladministration or appointing an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings. It can require the Commission to respond to questions and by a two-thirds majority can censure the whole Commission, as happened to the Santer Commission in 1999. In some cases, the Parliament has explicit consultation rights, which the Commission must genuinely follow. However, its role and participation in the legislative process still remains limited because no member can actually initiate or pass legislation without the Commission and Council, meaning power kratia is not in the hands of directly elected representatives of the people demos: in the EU it is not yet true that "the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the few."
syntax_complex.coling::049da962-b4ab-4271-80d7-6c08dd71: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics, which he directed against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, theologians appear to agree that Luther, adhering firmly to tradition, maintained his commitment to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church. He held fast to the belief, never wavering throughout his ministry, that Mary was a perpetual virgin and the Theotokos or Mother of God. Special attention is given to the assertion that Luther, writing some three-hundred years before the dogmatization of the Immaculate Conception by Pope Pius IX in 1854, was a firm adherent of that view, accepting it without reservation. Others maintain that Luther in later years changed his position on the Immaculate Conception, which, at that time remaining undefined in the Church, allowed for debate, maintaining however the sinlessness of Mary throughout her life. For Luther, early in his life when he was still forming his theological perspectives, the Assumption of Mary was an understood fact, although he later stated that the Bible did not say anything about it and stopped celebrating its feast. Important to him was the belief, which he defended vigorously, that Mary and the saints do live on after death. "Throughout his career as a priest-professor-reformer, Luther preached, taught, and argued about the veneration of Mary with a verbosity that ranged from childlike piety to sophisticated polemics, demonstrating the complexity of his thought. His views are intimately linked to his Christocentric theology and its consequences for liturgy and piety." Luther, while revering Mary and honoring her unique role, came to criticize the "Papists" for blurring the line between high admiration of the grace of God wherever it is seen in a human being and religious service given to another creature. He considered the Roman Catholic practice of celebrating saints' days and making intercessory requests addressed especially to Mary and other departed saints to be idolatry, constituting false worship. His final thoughts on Marian devotion and veneration are preserved in a sermon preached at Wittenberg only a month before his death.
syntax_complex.coling::0b4651e6-8f56-467b-81ae-810fa781:
A digital signature, which functions as a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents, provides a recipient, when the prerequisites are satisfied, with very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity) and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Being a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, digital signatures are commonly used for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management software, and in other cases where detecting forgery or tampering is important.

Though digital signatures are often used to implement electronic signatures, which includes any electronic data carrying the intent of a signature, not all electronic signatures use digital signatures. Having legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Uruguay, Switzerland, Chile and the countries of the European Union, electronic signatures have gained widespread acceptance.

Employing asymmetric cryptography, digital signatures in many instances provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel, with properly implemented signatures giving the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. Being equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respects, properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, which are cryptographically based, must be implemented properly to be effective. They can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message while also claiming their private key remains secret. Further, some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid. Digitally signed messages, which may be anything representable as a bitstring, include examples such as electronic mail, contracts, or a message sent via some other cryptographic protocol.
syntax_complex.coling::203e204e-a867-4d1d-97e8-bdd789e6:
Speech recognition, which is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT), is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies enabling the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers, with the main benefit being searchability. Incorporating knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields, it represents a domain whose reverse process is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training," also called "enrollment," where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system, which then analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Systems that do not use training, being called "speaker-independent" systems, contrast with those using training, which are called "speaker dependent."

Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces such as voice dialing, exemplified by commands like "call home," call routing, illustrated by phrases such as "I would like to make a collect call," domotic appliance control, search key words, as when finding a podcast where particular words were spoken, simple data entry, involving tasks like entering a credit card number, preparation of structured documents, such as a radiology report, determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing for word processors or emails, and aircraft applications, usually termed direct voice input.

The term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker rather than what they are saying, whereby recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice, or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations, most recently benefiting from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published in the field but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.
syntax_complex.coling::9be05dd7-05a8-4b0e-a617-ae611f4d:
Control theory, being a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines, has as its objective the development of a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability, often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To accomplish this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required, one that monitors the controlled process variable (PV) and compares it with the reference or set point (SP). The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, or SP-PV error, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects which are also studied include controllability and observability. Control theory, used in control system engineering to design automation that has revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries, has also created new fields such as robotics.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram, in which the transfer function, also known as the system function or network function, serves as a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system.

Control theory, dating from the 19th century when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell, was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, all of whom contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria, and from 1922 onwards, by the development of PID control theory by Nicolas Minorsky.

Although a major application of mathematical control theory is in control systems engineering, which deals with the design of process control systems for industry, other applications range far beyond this. As the general theory of feedback systems, control theory is useful wherever feedback occurs, thus having applications in life sciences, computer engineering, sociology and operations research.
syntax_complex.coling::5293d27b-2991-4ca1-93ab-e336d0eb:
Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug, being most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently, but not necessarily, relies on computer modeling techniques, this type of modeling sometimes being referred to as computer-aided drug design. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. In addition to small molecules, biopharmaceuticals, including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies, are an increasingly important class of drugs, and computational methods for improving the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based therapeutics have also been developed.

The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design, that is, design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target. Although design techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, side effects, and others, that first must be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug. These other characteristics are often difficult to predict with rational design techniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical phases of drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence are more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, in vitro experiments, when complemented with computation methods, are increasingly used in early drug discovery to select compounds with more favorable ADME profiles, encompassing absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, as well as toxicological profiles.
syntax_complex.coling::d2400f57-c1e4-49a6-aaa9-1c92f181:
Data dredging, which is also known as data snooping or p-hacking,[a] constitutes the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives, a practice that is accomplished by performing many statistical tests on the data while only reporting those that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging, involving the testing of multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable—represents a methodologically problematic approach to statistical inference.

Conventional tests of statistical significance, being based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type, these being mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis, with this level of risk being called the significance. When large numbers of tests are performed, some producing false results of this type, 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, while 1% might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested, it becoming virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant even though this is misleading, since almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain, for example, some spurious correlations, researchers using data mining techniques, if they are not cautious, can be easily misled by these results.

Data dredging being an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem, one form occurs when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined.
syntax_complex.coling::772c8684-83a7-4b50-8a32-d059bec2:
Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), which is a private research university in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, traces its origins to one of its predecessors that was established in 1900 by Andrew Carnegie as the Carnegie Technical Schools, subsequently becoming the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1912 and beginning to grant four-year degrees in the same year. In 1967, the Carnegie Institute of Technology merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research, which had been founded in 1913 by Andrew Mellon and Richard B. Mellon and which was formerly a part of the University of Pittsburgh.[10] Carnegie Mellon University, having undergone this merger, has operated as a single institution since that time.

The university consists of seven colleges and independent schools: The College of Engineering, College of Fine Arts, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Mellon College of Science, Tepper School of Business, Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, and the School of Computer Science.[11][12] The university, maintaining its main campus located 5 miles (8 km) from Downtown Pittsburgh, also has over a dozen degree-granting locations spanning six continents, including degree-granting campuses in Qatar, Silicon Valley, and Kigali, Rwanda (Carnegie Mellon University Africa), as well as partnerships with universities across the United States and in the United Kingdom, Portugal, Japan, China, Mexico, and Italy.[13]

Carnegie Mellon is known for its advances in research and new fields of study, notably being home to many firsts in computer science, including the first computer science, machine learning, and robotics departments, while pioneering the field of management science[14] and being home to the first drama program in the United States. CMU, which is classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very High Research Activity,"[15] had research and development expenditures of $386 million in 2020.[16] Past and present faculty and alumni include 20 Nobel Prize laureates, 13 Turing Award winners, 26 members of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 39 fellows of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, 91 members of the National Academies, 142 Emmy Award winners, 52 Tony Award laureates, and 12 Academy Award winners.[17] Carnegie Mellon, enrolling 15,818 students across its multiple campuses from 117 countries, employs more than 1,400 faculty members and has an active alumni base of over 112,000.[18]

Yes, although you wish your mother was sweet, gentle, understanding, and kind, you must not be disrespectful no matter what circumstances arise, making sure you don't verbalize your feelings in front of her since doing so will only make things worse for you. There's a very good chance that your mother knows she's not very smart, which makes her behave in mean ways, and reminding her of her shortcomings will not make life easier for you in any way whatsoever.

After you've given yourself the permission to cry, yell, scream, and express whatever you need to express, you should step away from your emotions completely. One of the more constructive ways to deal with your mother, which involves maintaining emotional detachment, means approaching her without anger, whining, crying, begging, yelling, or belittling—using just facts instead. If she intentionally does things to hurt you or make you angry, knowing what she's trying to accomplish, your best defense and offense combined is not letting yourself feel hurt or angry in response to her provocations.

Insofar as possible, do what she wants you to do before she even asks for it, which gives her one less thing to be mean about while simultaneously giving you the upper hand when you ask for what you want from her.

Pay close attention to the ideas of friends' mothers who are more gentle, consistent, and responsible, getting outside information that counteracts what you hear at home. Much of what you're being told every day is sabotaging and may be wrong, so instead of just getting mad at her for steering you wrong, you should seek sources of better information and remember what they say for future reference. Question anything she says about you or about life, comparing it with what ministers, therapists, teachers, and healthier adults say in similar situations. Examine everything in your life carefully because these things don't blow up out of nowhere but rather get passed on by generations, and you don't want to continue the cycle that has damaged so many.

This family dynamic can be studied, even in books that help you understand the patterns while choosing your own path in life. It may make her even angrier if you don't respond to the usual mind games in the usual way that she expects, but it's important to build some inner resistance to protect your mind and soul from further harm.

Don't be surprised if you get accused of things you wouldn't even think of doing—if she does them herself, she expects you to do them whether you would or not, projecting her own behavior onto you unfairly.
