Ask your doctor, who can provide specific guidance for your situation, if you are supposed to take your usual morning medications on the day of the procedure. If you have diabetes, which requires careful management of blood sugar levels, ask if you can take insulin or oral blood sugar medications before the test takes place. Tell your doctor if you have a history of asthma, kidney problems, or bleeding disorders, all of which may affect how the procedure is performed. Special precautions may be needed if you have one of these conditions, since they can increase the risk of complications during or after the angiogram.

You may be asked not to take aspirin, including other products that contain aspirin, or prescription blood thinners for several days before the test is scheduled. Discuss with your doctor, who understands your complete medical history, when you can resume these medications after the procedure has been completed.

Pregnant women, whose bodies are undergoing significant changes, need to be cautious about doing certain things to avoid harming the fetus that is developing inside them. If you are or might be pregnant, or if you just had a baby and are still in the postpartum period, discuss these details with your doctor so that you can decide together on the best course of action that protects both you and your child. It is extremely important to tell your doctor if you are pregnant because an angiogram, which involves radiation exposure, is needed to detect a potential coronary artery blockage that could be life-threatening. This may result in the need for reperfusion stenting, a procedure designed to restore blood flow to the heart muscle.

Use formula for one to two days after your angiogram if you are breast-feeding, continuing this practice until the dye that was injected during the procedure has passed completely through your body and is no longer present in your breast milk.

Your doctor, who has reviewed your medical history, will determine what testing you need to undergo before your angiogram takes place. Make sure you follow your doctor's directions carefully and complete any recommended testing that has been ordered. You may need to have blood taken for laboratory analysis or an electrocardiogram done before the angiogram is performed.

Iodine dye, which helps create clear images of blood vessels, is usually used in the cardiac catheterization test that comprises the angiogram. Your doctor will need to know if you possess such an allergy, which could cause a dangerous reaction, so you can explore other treatment options that are safer for you. Other possible dyes can cause a reaction in those allergic to shellfish, since shellfish proteins share similarities with certain contrast agents.

Most angiograms are planned for the morning hours, so this requirement shouldn't be a huge inconvenience for patients. But it is an important part of preparing for your angiogram, helping to ensure accurate results. If your test is scheduled for later in the day, do not consume any food or drink for four to eight hours before the test begins.

In the hours preceding your procedure, especially the twenty-four hours ahead of time when your body should be in optimal condition, you should avoid alcohol and tobacco products entirely. These substances can inhibit your behavior, alter test results significantly, and cause other complications during the procedure that could affect outcomes. If you are given a sedative during the procedure to help you relax, this could intensify the effects of any alcohol remaining in your system.

It is important to tell your doctor about any medications you are taking, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, herbs, and supplements, all of which may interact with the procedure. Bring them in their original bottles so your medical team can see exactly what you're taking. This will help you remember to tell the doctor about all the medications you are on without forgetting anything important. Remember to also notify the doctor about any medications you might be allergic to, since these allergies must be documented.

Even though the angiogram is a relatively simple procedure that is performed frequently, you will need to come to the hospital ready for a surgery, preparing yourself mentally and physically. Some ways to prepare yourself include following your doctor's instructions on what to eat and drink in the twenty-four hours leading up to your procedure, which may include not eating or drinking anything in the six to eight hours leading up to when your procedure begins. Other preparations involve removing your contact lenses, eyeglasses, hair clips, nail polish, and jewelry before the test, leaving your jewelry at home if possible. Emptying your bladder before the test is also important because the procedure can take several hours to complete.

At the hospital you'll need to check in at the registration desk and meet with your medical team, who will discuss exactly what will happen during the procedure so that you feel prepared and informed. They will let you know about any possible complications or risks that might occur.

You'll be taken to a room where you can change into a hospital gown, removing your street clothes, before the procedure begins.

After most angiograms, patients stay at the facility for four to six hours after the procedure has been completed. This is so that the staff can observe you carefully and make sure there are no postoperative complications developing. During this time, which may feel long, try to relax as much as possible. Don't let yourself stress about the results, which will be discussed with you later. Just enjoy taking a break while the doctors are there to watch you and ensure your safety.

You may be given a sedative during the angiogram procedure or immediately before it begins. This sedative, which helps you remain calm, will impair your ability to function normally and to operate a motor vehicle safely.

You'll need someone to give you a ride home and help you get settled in after your procedure is finished. Try to find someone you trust who can stay with you for a couple hours, preferably overnight, after you get home in case you need help with anything important. Most medical facilities will refuse to perform an angiogram on you if you do not have a responsible adult with you who has agreed to take you home safely.

One of the best ways to help your body recover from any kind of procedure is to get as much rest as possible, allowing healing to occur. This will help your body heal properly and avoid any potential complications that might arise. After the procedure, you'll probably feel a little discomfort in your groin area where the catheter was inserted. Bed rest will help you avoid moving that area unnecessarily so it can heal properly without disruption.

You should probably plan on staying home for a few days after the procedure to help you take it easy and recover fully.

Talk to your doctor about any questions or other concerns about the procedure that you may have. Tell them how you're feeling physically and emotionally and about any problems you may have encountered during recovery.

Ask your doctor about the outcome of the test and what the results mean for you moving forward with your treatment. Are more tests required to gather additional information? Do you need an operation to correct problems that were found? Should you change some aspect of your lifestyle to improve your health?

Black bears and grizzly bears, being distinct species, require different deterrents, so stay alert and avoid coming between a bear and her cub.

A black bear, which can actually be black, brown or cinnamon colored, is usually smaller, having pointier ears and lacking a hump that characterizes other species.

A grizzly bear, being brown, blonde or even slightly silver, has a hump on their back, possesses a dish shaped face and rounder ears, and when full-grown, is bigger than black bears.

Having a sense of smell that is extremely acute, they are constantly foraging in the summer and fall months, seeking food sources that will sustain them.

Bear spray, which is a type of pepper spray that creates a 30-foot (9 m) cone of spray, is only to be used when a bear is charging at you to change its direction, deterring the animal from continuing its approach.

Keeping your bear spray within arms reach while learning where the trigger is in advance will prepare you for an encounter.

Pull the trigger when the bear, approaching rapidly, is within 40 feet (12 m) of you, creating a barrier between yourself and the animal.

Never use bear spray as a preventative measure, since it is extremely potent and should not be sprayed on equipment or used in any situation other than an actual charge.

Making noise while hiking will help avoid encounters, as grizzly and black bears, hearing unfamiliar sounds, try to avoid this sound that signals human presence.

Bear bells, being usually too quiet to keep bears away, are ineffective, but human conversation, which carries farther and is more distinctive, will do the trick.

Don't hike alone in bear country, since bears are more likely to approach an individual than a group, and if you don't want to talk constantly, carry a satellite radio and set it to a talk show, creating continuous noise.

Running from bears, which run up to 35 mph (56 km/h), far faster than humans, is futile, and they can also follow you up trees or into water, making escape nearly impossible.

Camping upwind means the bear will smell you and keep away, though if you haven't hidden your food in an airtight, bear-safe container, this positioning could work to your disadvantage.

If you encounter a bear, stand your ground and make noise while avoiding eye contact, remaining calm and assertive.

Bears, which may stand on their hind legs to get a better look at you, are often simply investigating, but it's best to be confident and stand your ground during such moments.

If a small black bear attacks you, you may be able to fight back effectively.

If a grizzly bear attacks you, curl up in the fetal position, keeping your hands laced behind your back, protecting your neck, because if the bear realizes you are not a threat or dead, it may walk away peacefully.

Remember that bear attacks, despite popular fears, are rare occurrences.

Pick a time when they are in a good mood, avoiding any approach right after they've had a hard day at work. Try to figure out their mood by asking, "How was your day?" while simultaneously choosing a time when you will not be interrupted or competing for their attention with other people or issues that might be demanding their focus. Right after dinner or before bed is usually a pretty peaceful and private time that works well for these types of conversations.

If you don't get a chance at home, you can also be more creative and talk with them while out on a walk or even while riding in the car, which provides a more casual setting. You might say, "Dad, do you want to go on a quick walk? I have some things I'd like to talk with you about," framing the request in a way that feels natural and inviting. You can always talk with just one parent too and ask them to approach the other one, if needed, which is a strategy that works best if you know your mom, for example, is a bit more lenient or if you feel closer to her and believe she'll be more receptive to your concerns.

Staying honest and straightforward is just one way to show your maturity, demonstrating that you understand the importance of integrity in family relationships. So, don't tell lies, even white lies that might seem harmless at the moment. If you've already gone on a date with this guy, you might as well tell them now, if they ask, since concealing information will only complicate matters later. If you are caught in a lie you will lose any ground that you've gained, undermining all the trust you've been working to build.

Another part of honesty is your being open to their concerns so you can respond to them in a thoughtful and considered manner. For example, if they don't trust your boyfriend because they don't know him very well, try to create more opportunities for everyone to get to know each other, which can help alleviate their worries and build bridges between all parties involved.

Avoid comparing yourself with others if it involves exaggeration, as this tactic often backfires and damages your credibility. For example, don't tell your parents that your best friend has had a boyfriend for the past two years, unless it is really true and you can verify this fact. Your parents will sense that you are not being honest and can easily check the facts, which will undermine your position entirely.

To get what you want, you may have to give a little, understanding that negotiation involves compromise on both sides. If your parents agree to let you have a boyfriend, they will most likely place some conditions on their agreement that reflect their concerns about your wellbeing. If these are promises that you can actually keep, it is best to say yes and demonstrate your reliability. You can also bring up compromises as a way to bring your parents back to the bargaining table if they say no initially, showing that you're willing to work within reasonable boundaries.

This will create an opening for greater freedom in the future as you gain their trust through consistent behavior and responsible choices.

Many of the conditions will involve your performance at school, which is an area where they feel they can measure your maturity. For example, you must keep a certain GPA to have a boyfriend, or you need to spend at least one hour each night studying without distraction. These are all goals that you should have anyway, so there is no harm in agreeing to them since they support your long-term success.

It is likely that they will also try to limit your time with your new boyfriend, out of an effort to keep you from getting in over your head emotionally or losing focus on other important priorities. They may ask you to only go out once a week or to stick to a strict curfew that ensures you're home at a reasonable hour.

They may also want you to see and talk with a health professional who can provide guidance on relationships and related topics. You will need to decide individually if you are comfortable with this type of compromise, weighing the benefits against any concerns you might have.

Try to control your emotions during your talk, recognizing that composure will serve you better than any emotional outburst. Avoid yelling, crying, whining, or begging, since a temper tantrum of any kind will make them lose all respect for your position and view you as immature. To stay calm, repeat in your head the word "control" or "calm," using it as a mantra. Count for five seconds, in your head, before you answer any questions or make any statements you may regret later.

Make sure to watch your tone as well, being aware that it is really easy to say nice words with a sarcastic attitude that undermines your message. For example, "That's great," sounds really different depending on your tone of voice, which can convey either genuine agreement or dismissive mockery. If you feel increasingly frustrated by the conversation, plan a way to blow off some steam after it concludes. Visualize taking a long run, swimming some laps, or going shopping with friends, activities that will help you decompress.

Your parents will most likely have quite a bit to say back to you, so make sure to pay close attention to what they are saying rather than simply waiting for your turn to speak. Look into their eyes when they are talking, which will help to show that you are not embarrassed or ashamed to talk about your possible relationship and that you value their input. Nod your head when they make good points and even smile if you really agree with something they've said.

A big part of active listening is asking questions that demonstrate genuine engagement with their perspective. If they say no to you, respond by asking, "Why not?" in a respectful tone. Tell them that you honestly want to understand their perspective in this situation, which will help you to figure out what is bothering them so you can work on it and potentially address their concerns.

If you haven't already discussed it, your parents may want to sit down with you at a later time to discuss their concerns about you having sex, which is a natural extension of the boyfriend conversation. Again, this 'sex talk' could actually be really useful for you, providing information you need. This will be a safe time for you to ask questions or express concerns about topics that might otherwise be difficult to bring up.

If you just can't talk to your parents face-to-face, you may need to write down your feelings and thoughts via a letter that gives you time to organize your arguments carefully. This is also a good idea if you think your parents may have an extreme reaction to your request that could derail productive conversation.

Make sure that your letter is well written and calm, reflecting the maturity you want them to recognize. Do not write anything that you will regret once they've read it and had time to process your words. Instead of saying, "I'm going to have a boyfriend whether you like it or not," which sounds confrontational and disrespectful, you might write, "I really want you to understand where I'm coming from," which invites dialogue.

It may be helpful to show your letter to a trusted friend or family member for feedback before presenting it to your parents, ensuring that your tone and message are appropriate.

Trapdoor spiders are approximately 0.79 in to 1.26 inches (1 to 3 cm) long, which means roughly between the size of your pinky nail and your thumbnail. Trapdoor spiders, being black or brown with stout bodies and legs, sometimes have paler color markings on some species, or they may have a silky covering of hair that gives them a distinctive appearance. Their bodies, which are divided into two sections—the thorax (containing the head and legs) and the abdomen—typically display an abdomen that is lighter and a slightly different color from the rest of the body.

Though they may be difficult to see because of its small size, a trapdoor spider will have 6 eyes arranged in 3 groups, whereas most other spiders have 8 eyes, making this a distinguishing characteristic. Trapdoor spiders, being relatives of tarantulas, are nevertheless less hairy and have smaller, shinier bodies than their larger cousins. The jaws of a trapdoor spider, which are attached to the front of its head, move up and down, unlike most other spiders whose jaws move side to side, representing another unique anatomical feature.

Females trapdoor spiders, being larger than the males, are seldom seen because they rarely leave their burrows, meaning that if you see a trapdoor spider, it is most likely a male. Look for these characteristics that identify male trapdoor spiders: short and blunt spinnerets, which produce silk and are located at the tip of the abdomen; a double spur about halfway along their front legs; a dusty or dull carapace (a harder area covering much of the thorax) that is lightly covered in bristles; and pedipalps (small appendages near the jaws) that resemble boxing gloves.

There are numerous varieties of trapdoor spiders, each with slightly different physical characteristics, and more varieties of trapdoor spiders are still being discovered through ongoing research. If you think you have seen a trapdoor spider, look up the specific varieties that live in your area so that you can know what kind of specific markings to expect when identifying specimens.

The geographic distribution of trapdoor spiders, being erratic and attributed to the continental drift that occurred millions of years ago, means that various species of trapdoor spiders can be found all over the world. Look for trapdoor spiders in North America, including Canada and The United States (southeastern and pacific states, and north to Colorado), as well as Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, etc.), Asia (China, Japan, Thailand, etc.), South Africa and Madagascar, and Australia.

Throughout the world, trapdoor spiders favor warm environments, such as temperate forests and deserts, and they will burrow in grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt embankments where conditions are suitable. Trapdoor spiders burrow in the ground (about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep) and cover their burrow with a silken hinged "trapdoor" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material, making the burrows very hard to see because they are so well camouflaged. Larger burrows may have multiple trapdoors, and usually, the burrow faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation that provides cover.

Trapdoor spiders, being shy and possibly nocturnal, are rarely seen far from their burrows, though males may wander during mating season. You might be able to spy one, however, when it eats, as the spiders will wait in their burrows until they sense vibrations in the ground caused by insects (including crickets, moths, beetles, and grasshoppers) and other spiders, at which point the spiders will leap out of the trapdoor, grab one of these animals, and drag it back into the burrow for consumption.

Wipe your knee with a damp washcloth and, if necessary, a mild soap, making sure to wash away grease, sweat, and any soap residue before drying your knee thoroughly, since ensuring that your knee is clean and dry will help prevent irritation from developing. You can also shave the area 12 hours prior to taping if it will be taped repeatedly, which will help reduce pain when the tape is removed later.

Lie with your back propped up or supported and legs outstretched in front of you, positioning yourself so that your knees remain completely relaxed and slightly bent throughout the process. To help keep your knee bent and relaxed in this optimal position, place a rolled towel under it for support.

You'll use rigid sports tape to perform the actual McConnell technique, but because sports tape can be irritating and uncomfortable against bare skin, you should first cover your entire knee with a strip of low irritant, hypoallergenic tape as a protective barrier. A permeable, breathable white cotton tape serves as a good underwrap option for this purpose.

Use a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your kneecap, which will define your work surface on the underwrap layer and make it easier to apply the sports tape properly, allowing you to actually see the kneecap's boundaries clearly marked beneath.

Use non-stretch adhesive sports tape for the McConnell technique, cutting a two to three inch (five to eight cm) strip, or enough tape to cover your knee from outer to inner edges completely. Sports tape with a width of 38 mm (1.5 inches) is the best size for knee taping applications.

Apply one end of the tape to the outer edge of your kneecap so the tape is vertically centered with the knee, adhering the tape to your skin in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner of your knee while using your thumb to gently push the kneecap toward the inside of the leg simultaneously.

While moving the kneecap and applying the tape in this manner, use your fingers to carefully pull the skin on the inside of your leg toward the kneecap, since your goal is to push the kneecap toward the inside of your leg, wrinkle the skin there so it meets the kneecap, and use the tape to hold them tightly together in this corrected position.

Place one edge of the second strip of tape on the outer edge of your knee and, again, make sure it's vertically centered with your kneecap before securing the tape to your skin in a straight, horizontal motion that creates a straight line from the outside of your knee to the inside. Apply one to three more layers of tape until you feel your desired level of tightness and support has been achieved.

Make sure you've created skin wrinkles on the inside part of your knee, wrinkles that should run vertically, or up and down, and that you should be able to see through the underlay, since wrinkling of the skin results when you pull the kneecap inward and secure it to the skin on the inside of the leg properly.

Wear the tape during physical activity as directed by your physical therapist or another medical professional, though in general, you should remove the tape within 48 hours of application to avoid complications. As strength, range of motion, and balance improve over time, keep the knee taped for shorter periods of time during general activities, working towards taping it only for higher risk activities, like sports participation.

Hold your kneecap as you slowly peel off the tape to prevent worsening an injury that may exist, placing your fingers as close as you can to the tape's line of attachment, or where it meets your skin, following the line with your fingers as you pull the strip of tape to guide it off of your skin gently, since pulling too fast can cause skin irritation or abruptly force the kneecap out of position.

Remove the tape immediately if it worsens your pain or causes concerning symptoms, taking the tape off if you experience discoloration, pins and needles, or swelling after applying the tape. Tell your physical therapist or other medical professional about these or any other adverse symptoms that result from taping, keeping in mind that it's best to consult a medical professional before taping, especially if you have circulatory problems, a knee fracture, or are allergic to sports tape materials.

Corfe Castle railway station, which is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle in the English county of Dorset, was originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line that ran from Wareham to Swanage, though the line and station, having been closed by British Rail in 1972, have since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, being a heritage railway that runs from Norden station, situated just north of Corfe Castle, to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle stands on a railway line that connects Wareham and Norden.

History
Corfe Castle, lying in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, occupies a peninsula that is bordered by the English Channel to the south and by the marshy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area surrounding Corfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn tramways—these being the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway—to wharves located on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage, positioned at the tip of the Isle, was equally well known for the Purbeck Marble that was mined locally and subsequently shipped out by sea.

The presence of these industries attracted railway promoters once the L&SWR main line, having reached Wareham in 1847, made the area accessible by rail. Several schemes were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway, receiving its Act in 1881, opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle, commanding the only relatively low level route that crossed the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the line passed close to the centre of the village, with Corfe Castle station being built for the opening of the line. From its opening, the line, which was operated by the L&SWR, was absorbed into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station, being the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch, retained this status until its closure by British Rail and possessed the only passing loop situated between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, having probably been present from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the allocated coach, being a camping coach that had been converted from a Pullman car fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room containing two single beds, was stationed here, with two of these coaches being present from 1962 until 1967.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the line, the collapse of both the clay and marble industries, combined with the increase in private car ownership occurring during the second half of the 20th century, made the line unprofitable. Closure, having been first proposed in 1967, was finally implemented on 3 January 1972 despite local opposition. During the final few years of the line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units, which were also known as type 2H.

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route passing through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway, having started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982, continued to expand its operations.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site that had been built on the former location of the exchange sidings situated between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden station was built, with most trains now terminating at this location. Corfe Castle station, having reopened on 12 August 1995, did not receive its official opening until February of the following year.

A 5-year project undertaken by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening. The footbridge, having been originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway and featuring cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until it was removed by Swanage Railway volunteers. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station, being safer and more convenient for the public than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing. The project, winning the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007, received a plaque that was presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, who served as Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to and from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole while the other proceeded to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail services running on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018 and 2019, these being operated by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day running in each direction. However, in July 2019 these services were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services operating to Corfe Castle.

Services
Services run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation occurring in March, November and December. The level of service, varying from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction depending on the season and the day of the week, provides comprehensive coverage. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross, requiring 10 minutes, Herston, where trains stop only on request, and Swanage, taking 21 minutes. Northbound, trains operate to Norden station, which is reached in 3 minutes.

Museum
Corfe Castle station, being also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, houses the collection in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The museum, opening on most operating days, welcomes visitors throughout the season.

The museum includes Secundus, being a narrow gauge steam locomotive that was built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This locomotive, having been in use until 1955, was then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the locomotive will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, which is currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway station.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon that was directed by Earl Duvall, with the short being released on February 17, 1934.

The film, which was supervised by Earl Duvall, featured characters animated by Jack King and Frank Tipper, both of whom were credited, as well as Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, the final four remaining uncredited. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown, who was solely credited, and Norman Spencer, who was solely uncredited, while the sound was solely recorded by Bernard Brown, whose contribution in this capacity went uncredited. Production number 6125.

Plot
The cartoon follows a male and female bug/insect who check into a hotel which subsequently catches on fire.

Music
The song "Honeymoon Hotel," which was written by Al Dubin and Harry Warren, was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade, and this short appears on the DVD release of that film.

Color process
The film is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon that was produced in color, using Cinecolor since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor, namely Beauty and the Beast, before the series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes continued being produced in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.

Modern Greek art, which emerged during the period between the establishment of the new independent Greek state and the arrival of the 20th century, is art that reflects the nation's renewed cultural identity.

Since Mainland Greece, having been under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, was not a part of the Renaissance and the artistic movements that followed in Western Europe, it found itself separated from these transformative developments. However, Greek islands such as Crete, and the Ionian islands in particular, being under Venetian or other European powers' rule for large periods, were able to better assimilate the radical artistic changes that were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th century, thereby maintaining closer contact with Western artistic evolution.

The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art, which followed parallel routes to Western Europe, are two important artistic movements in Greece that contributed significantly to the nation's cultural heritage.

Modern Greek art, shaped predominantly by the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece, the large Greek diaspora that existed across Europe, and the new Greek social elite that emerged following independence, can be said to have been influenced as well by external artistic forces, predominantly from Germany and France, which exerted considerable pressure on artistic development.

Sculpture and painting

19th century

The School of Munich

Modern Greek art, which began to be developed around the time of Romanticism when nationalist sentiments were running high, witnessed Greek artists absorbing many elements from their European colleagues, resulting in the culmination of the distinctive style of Greek Romantic art, inspired not only by revolutionary ideals but also by the country's geography and history, which provided rich thematic material. After centuries of Ottoman rule had ended, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the newly independent Greece, making studying abroad imperative for artists who sought professional training. Munich, being an important international center for the arts at that time and offering comprehensive academic programs, was the place where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study, seeking to master European techniques. In the school of Munich, which was led by Karl von Piloty, true fresco was taught specifically for mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster, preserving traditional methods. During this period, much of the art, reflecting the emotional climate of the era, was emotional and theatrical in tone, appealing to viewers' sentiments. The most prominent themes of the school of Munich, addressing diverse aspects of existence, were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape, all rendered with technical precision.

Later on, having completed their studies and absorbed European artistic principles, they would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge to younger generations eager to learn. Some of them, choosing to extend their careers abroad, remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar, where they contributed to the city's cosmopolitan atmosphere. Both academic and personal bonds, which developed between early Greek painters and Munich artistry through years of collaboration and mutual influence, gave birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting, a distinctive synthesis of traditions. Nikolaos Gysis, who was an important teacher and artist at the Munich Academy where he trained numerous students, soon became a leading figure among Greek artists working in Germany. Academism, realism, genre painting, upper middle class portraiture, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features that captured fleeting moments, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are mainly traced in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others who embraced these newer aesthetic movements. Early-20th-century modernism, breaking with traditional forms, is also represented by significant Greek artists in Munich who pushed boundaries. Many of these Munich School artists, seeking to connect with their heritage while abroad, chose subjects such as everyday Greek life, local customs, and living conditions that reflected authentic experiences. Several important painters, each developing distinctive approaches, emerged at this time with varying specializations. Theodoros Vryzakis, who specialized in historical painting that commemorated national achievements, was especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence that established the modern nation. Nikiphoros Lytras, pursuing a different direction, concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life that captured ordinary moments. Georgios Jakobides, who devoted his attention to infants and children with tender sensitivity, would later become the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens, guiding institutional development. Georgios Roilos, who was another leading painter of the period closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career before exploring other directions, contributed significantly to Greek artistic identity. Konstantinos Volanakis, whose maritime subjects reflected Greece's relationship with water, was inspired mostly by the Greek sea that surrounded the nation.

Other artists who were associated with the School of Munich included Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico, all of whom contributed to Greek art's evolution.

Notable sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom, working in three dimensions, were Leonidas Drosis (his major work being the extensive neo-classical architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens that adorned the building), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis, each contributing to public monuments.

The School of Paris

A few Greek painters, seeking alternative training, studied in Paris where different traditions prevailed. Despite residing in the French capital and following the guidelines of the French Art Academy, which emphasized classical principles, they invariably had their own interpretations that reflected Greek sensibilities. Jacob Rizos, focusing on feminine subjects, was involved with the rendering of female grace through delicate compositions, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East that depicted regional culture, and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, still life and genre painting that showcased technical versatility. During this period in Paris, the avant-garde Impressionist movement, which revolutionized approaches to light and color, developed rapidly, but most Greek painters, remaining conservative in their approach, remained faithful to the precepts of their teachers with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement that suggested future possibilities. The first Greek impressionist, breaking with academic tradition, was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris where he initially trained, settled in Belgium and became a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte, participating in progressive artistic circles.

Themes-artistic depictions

Many Greek artists of this period, looking to historical precedents for inspiration, also drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes that required spiritual gravity. This tied in with the idea of modern secular Greek art of the period referencing more classical styles drawn from antiquity, while religious art, maintaining devotional traditions, referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art that preserved sacred aesthetics. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role, contributing to artistic development, was played by artists from Ionian islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, who exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers to create distinctive works. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives that reflected changing times, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century, seeking to establish national identity, reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition, as well as with the quests of the European ateliers, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Greek contemporary art of the period, showcasing this synthesis, including the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras who exemplified these dual influences.

20th century

At the beginning of the 20th century, landscape painting, which emphasized natural beauty, held sway and the interest of painters, shifting from historical subjects, turned toward the study of light and color as primary concerns. The dependence of Munich, which had dominated earlier, slackened considerably and Paris, offering new artistic movements, became the pole of attraction for the artists of the period who sought contemporary approaches. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, who was a contemporary and friend of Picasso during formative years, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto" through his work. Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos, working in multiple media, achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of painting and poetry that combined visual and verbal expression, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis, responding to social conditions, became associated with European critical realism that addressed contemporary issues. Impressionism, representing modern sensibility, was the original influence on the leading figures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, both masters of color, while Nikiphoros Lytras, maintaining connections abroad, associated himself with the avant-garde groups of Munich constituting the last known link with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art that had shaped previous generations. The further development of these painters, exploring personal visions, led to other roads, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Greek dimension that distinguished their work.

Gradually the impressionists and other modern schools, gaining prominence internationally, increased their influence on Greek practitioners. In the early 20th century Greek artists, seeking new inspiration and training, turned from Munich to Paris where modernism flourished. The interest of Greek painters, artists, reflecting broader cultural changes, changes from historical representations to Greek landscapes with an emphasis on light and colours so abundant in Greece's Mediterranean environment. Representatives of this artistic change, pioneering new approaches, are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis, each contributing distinctive innovations. Konstantinos Parthenis, who in particular introduces historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Greek painting into modern art while maintaining national character, exemplifies this synthesis. The same is true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas, who rendered nature with vibrant intensity, and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis, whose emotional approach conveyed psychological depth. The period of the 1930s, representing a culmination of earlier developments, was a landmark for the Greek painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (who introduced abstraction in Greek paintings, breaking with representational traditions) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Greek Art with varied contributions. These painters, seeking to establish Greek modernism, tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition, creating a distinctive synthesis.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists

The second half of the 20th century, extending into recent decades, has seen a range of acclaimed Greek artists working in diverse media, such as Constantine Andreou, who was recipient of the French Légion d'honneur for artistic achievement, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor whose work garnered widespread recognition. Giorgio de Chirico, who was an influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter creating enigmatic compositions, founded Metaphysical art that influenced subsequent movements. Jannis Kounellis, working with unconventional materials, ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement that challenged traditional practices. Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor working with technology, is the most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motion, creating immersive environments. Theodoros Stamos, who was a renowned abstract expressionist painter creating gestural compositions, contributed to international movements. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis, all of whom achieved international recognition, are internationally acclaimed artists of Kinetic sculpture who explored movement and space. Other notable Greek artists, continuing these traditions, are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis, all contributing to contemporary practice.

syntax_complex.coling::bb048a1e-39f8-4c80-9db0-70176b1c: Grace Files The Department Break-Room, which serves as our communal gathering space, is always a fun place where we can unwind. Its employees, people like me who have dedicated themselves to this eternal service, all share one little gift that was bestowed upon us by the Chief Executive: Immortality that stretches forward without end. So long as we continue to do our jobs with the diligence that's expected of us, we're given all the time we could ever want or need to exist and work. A large chunk of that infinite existence, usually amounting to a bit less than three quarters of it when you calculate the proportions, is spent working at our assigned tasks. This is mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment, creating an endless stream of work. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, which you might think would make everything easier, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble processing all the people who are dying across every moment of human history. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus, enjoying whatever recreational activities suit our preferences, and that leads to another fun thing that being immortal causes: you get people from everywhere and everywhen you can think of mixing together in ways that would be impossible otherwise. One of the older reapers, who has been with the Department for millennia, was around when the Aztec Empire was basically a handful of guys with an insane idea involving a cactus, a snake, and an eagle coming together. Another of us, who carries the bearing of ancient Rome in his posture, was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed in that famous betrayal. You get a lot of weird interactions when you mix in so many people from such vastly different eras and cultures. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race from back when the Empire was at its height, cheering as though it were happening live. The Aztec is chatting with a Norseman, both of them discussing with surprising academic interest the merits of hanging as opposed to cutting the heart out as a method of ritual sacrifice. Some of the Americans, such as myself who hail from various decades of that nation's history, are chatting about college sports around a water cooler, debating teams and games with the passion of true fans, and the younger members of our staff, those who died in the digital age, are setup in the region we call "The Arcade," where they play games that remind them of their former lives. After all those people scattered throughout the Break-Room... there's the guy at the bar who stands apart from everyone else. He's the oldest of the Reapers, a figure shrouded in mystery and speculation. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone who's asked, and his records are covered up by administrative seals that nobody can access. He doesn't get out much from whatever duties occupy his time, but we've all seen him milling around the Department on rare occasions. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar where others gather to drink and socialize. We've got every drink imagined, at least up until the present day out on Earth, available for anyone who wants them. I took a seat next to him, settling onto the barstool with curiosity driving my actions. "Evening," I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me since Language barriers don't exist for Reapers, allowing us to hear everything in our native language regardless of when or where the speaker originated. Everyone hears us in their native language as well, which leads to all kinds of insanity in the modern world where people speak hundreds of tongues... or when we talk to people in Ancient Greece or Rome who've been dead for thousands of years. "Evening," the Eldest said, acknowledging my greeting. His voice sounded deep and ancient, like stones grinding together in the earth. "What are you drinking to," I asked, curious about what could drive this mysterious figure to seek solace in alcohol. "Death," the Eldest said without hesitation or irony. I didn't laugh, and neither did he, because there was nothing funny about it. "Whose?" I asked, wanting to understand. "Millions," he said with a weight that conveyed centuries of experience. I nodded in reply, understanding what he meant. Reapers may be immortal, and we may have a lot of not-quite-natural abilities that set us apart from ordinary humans, but we're all still human at our core where it matters most. Our minds are just like the minds of the people we reap, subject to the same emotional tolls and psychological pressures, and doing our job is rough in ways that are hard to articulate. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world, or any world for that matter... having to be there when someone's dying and watching them slip away. Seeing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer, or other diseases that ravage their bodies, and having to deliver a bitter mercy to spare someone the pain of lingering is soul-crushing. That's not even thinking about the horrors you get when you walk into a combat zone to retrieve the deceased whose bodies are torn apart, or have to retrieve someone who succumbed to despair and ended their own life... Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten depressed over that burden, over not being able to help the dying beyond giving them the bitter mercy that is death itself. We're all human, and we all still have our empathy intact despite the centuries. I figured that the Eldest, despite his age and experience, had managed to experience that same crushing weight. "You talked to the Councilors about it?" I asked, hoping he'd sought help. The Councilors, who serve as our support system, aren't Reapers for the most part. They're among the Dead, the people who live in whatever comes next after mortal life ends. They're also volunteers who come into the Department to help us out with our mental hang-ups and emotional struggles. I know I spend a lot of time talking to 'em about my own issues. "No..." the guy said, pausing before adding, "at least... not this century." "Which deaths have you down?" I asked gently. "Fratricide..." the Reaper said, his voice breaking slightly, "It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much." I nodded, understanding the implication. Reapers come in all forms and from all backgrounds. Some of us are like me, and we took the job offer to get someone else a better afterlife than they would have had otherwise, making a sacrifice for love. Some are here serving to get themselves into something halfway decent after lives of sin. The Eldest was apparently among the latter group. "So," I said carefully, "You thought about requesting that those assignments be diverted to other Reapers who wouldn't be triggered?" "Can't..." he said firmly, "It's part of my... my sentence that was handed down." "Ouch," I said, and I genuinely meant it from the bottom of my heart. When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest who are working off debts, they have something called a Sentence which is designed to reform them to a state where they would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due to be sent to eventually. It's a set of obligations they must fulfil without deviation, or be sent on ahead of schedule to one of the... less desirable final rests that await the wicked. If they're lucky, they just get reincarnated to try again. If they're unlucky, they're supposed to get thrown into Torment for eternity. "It's just..." He said, struggling to articulate his pain, "I've seen so many of them over the centuries. Every time I go out on assignment... I don't see the person I'm sent for anymore. I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper when I was still mortal... and I see myself standing over them with blood on my hands." I saw a tear roll down the Eldest's cheek at those words, revealing vulnerability, and I remained silent because nothing I could say would help. "Damn it..." the Eldest said, composing himself with visible effort, "I need to get back to work... need to get out of here before I break down completely..." "Luck," I said quietly, "and consider scheduling an appointment soon. We don't need you going renegade and breaking your protocols. That generally results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us to process." The Eldest scoffed at that observation, recognizing the truth in it, and nodded in my direction as he got up to leave the bar. It was only once he'd left the room, disappearing into the corridors beyond, that I realized that I still didn't have his name.

Modern Greek art represents creations during the period between independence and modernism. The new Greek state emerged victoriously from Ottoman domination. Greece gained independence after the revolutionary war in the 1820s. The country established itself as a nation in that era.

Mainland Greece endured Ottoman rule for the preceding four centuries. The region missed the Renaissance entirely during that long occupation. Greece remained isolated from artistic movements in Western Europe. Ottoman control prevented participation in European cultural developments.

Greek islands experienced different historical circumstances during those same centuries. Crete remained under Venetian rule for extended periods. The Ionian islands accepted governance by various European powers. These islands absorbed radical artistic changes from continental Europe. Cultural exchange occurred naturally on the islands between the fourteenth and eighteenth centuries.

The Cretan School developed distinctive artistic characteristics during the Venetian period. The Heptanese School represented another important movement in Greek territories. These two movements followed parallel routes to Western Europe. Both schools maintained connections with European artistic developments.

Modern Greek art reflects the particular socioeconomic conditions within the nation. The large Greek diaspora spread families and artists across Europe. The new Greek social elite patronized artists after independence. External artistic influences came predominantly from Germany and France. These factors shaped Greek artistic development throughout the nineteenth century.

Greek artists began developing modern styles around the time of Romanticism. These creators absorbed many elements from their European colleagues. The distinctive style of Greek Romantic art culminated in this period. Revolutionary ideals inspired many paintings and sculptures across Greece. The country's geography and history provided endless subjects for artists.

Ottoman rule had limited opportunities for arts education over the centuries. The newly independent Greece lacked established academies for aspiring artists. Greek artists studied abroad out of necessity during this period. Munich represented an important international center for the arts. The majority of Greek artists chose Munich for their studies.

The school of Munich received direction from Karl von Piloty. True fresco technique was taught for mural paintings there. Artists learned to paint on fresh wet lime plaster. Much of the art conveyed emotional and theatrical qualities. The school of Munich emphasized urban life as a subject. Rural life appeared frequently in paintings from this school. Still life compositions attracted many Greek painters there. Landscape painting became another prominent theme in the curriculum.

Greek artists returned to Greece after completing their studies. These trained painters passed their knowledge to younger generations. Some artists remained in Munich throughout their productive careers. Munich earned the nickname Athens on the Isar. Academic bonds developed between Greek painters and Munich artistry. Personal relationships strengthened connections between the two artistic communities. The Greek Munich School of painting emerged from these connections.

Nikolaos Gysis became an important teacher at the Munich Academy. The artist achieved recognition as a leading figure among Greeks. Academism dominated the early years of the Greek school. Realism appeared in many works from this productive period. Genre painting attracted numerous practitioners during these prosperous decades. Upper middle class portraiture provided income for many artists. Still life paintings demonstrated technical skill in controlled compositions. Landscape painting often represented impressionist features in later works. Symbolism replaced earlier styles at the end of the century. Jugendstil appeared mainly in the work of Nikolaos Gysis. Art Nouveau traces can be found in Aristeas and others. Early twentieth century modernism attracted significant Greek artists in Munich.

Munich School artists chose subjects from everyday Greek life. Local customs appeared frequently in paintings from this period. Living conditions provided material for socially conscious artists throughout Greece. Several important painters emerged during these productive decades in Bavaria.

Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical painting for patriotic audiences. The 1821 Greek War of Independence inspired his compositions. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and children. He would later become the first Director at the National Gallery. Georgios Roilos represented another leading painter of the period. His work showed close association with the Munich School. Konstantinos Volanakis drew inspiration mostly from the Greek sea.

Other artists maintained associations with the School of Munich. Symeon Sabbides completed his training under Munich masters there. Yannoulis Chalepas studied sculpture with Germanic influences on technique. Leonidas Drosis worked in both painting and sculpture. Quite a few modernist artists studied in Munich. Theofrastos Triantafyllidis belonged to this younger generation of innovators. Jorgos Busianis explored modernist approaches to traditional Greek subjects. Giorgio de Chirico also studied briefly in the Bavarian capital.

Notable sculptors emerged in the new Greek Kingdom. Leonidas Drosis created extensive neoclassical architectural ornament at the Academy. Lazaros Sochos produced monumental works for public spaces. Georgios Vitalis specialized in portrait busts for wealthy patrons. Dimitrios Filippotis contributed sculptures to important civic buildings. Ioannis Kossos worked in traditional marble for classical subjects. Yannoulis Chalepas achieved recognition for innovative techniques in stone. Georgios Bonanos created religious sculptures for Orthodox churches. Lazaros Fytalis completed numerous commissions for public monuments.

A few Greek painters studied in Paris instead of Munich. These artists resided in the French capital for their training. They followed the guidelines of the French Art Academy. Greek painters invariably developed their own interpretations of academic rules. Jacob Rizos involved himself with the rendering of female grace. Theodoros Rallis depicted scenes from the Orthodox East. Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos concentrated on portraiture throughout his long career. Still life and genre painting also attracted his attention.

The avant garde Impressionist movement developed during this period. Most Greek painters remained faithful to academic precepts nonetheless. Only some nebulous thrusts appeared in the direction of Impressionism. Périclès Pantazis became the first Greek impressionist painter. He settled in Belgium after his time in Paris. Pantazis became a part of the Circle de la pâte.

Many Greek artists drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration. Religious themes particularly benefited from this Byzantine influenced approach. Modern secular Greek art referenced more classical styles deliberately. Religious art referenced Byzantine traditions or Byzantine inspired art. Artists from Ionian islands played an important pioneering role. These painters exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance effectively. Baroque ateliers provided additional training for ambitious Greek artists.

Greek artists reconnected their work with ancient tradition gradually. The quests of European ateliers influenced this reconnection significantly. The Munich School provided defining examples of Greek contemporary art. The works of Theodoros Vryzakis demonstrated this synthesis clearly. Nikiphoros Lytras also created defining examples of the period.

Landscape painting held sway at the beginning of the century. Painters turned their interest toward the study of light. Color became an obsession for the younger generation of artists. The dependence on Munich slackened considerably during this transitional period. Paris became the pole of attraction for Greek artists.

Demetrios Galanis achieved wide recognition in France early on. The critic Andre Malreaux acclaimed him as an artist capable of stirring emotions. Picasso maintained a contemporary friendship with Galanis throughout their careers. Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition later in the century. His surrealist conceptions encompassed both painting and poetry successfully. Dimitris Mytaras became associated with European critical realism eventually. Yiannis Psychopedis also embraced critical realism in the late sixties.

Impressionism influenced the leading figures of Greek art initially. Konstantinos Parthenis absorbed impressionist techniques in his early period. Konstantinos Maleas also studied impressionism during his formative years. Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with avant garde groups in Munich. His work constituted the last known link with Munich traditions.

Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris gradually. The interest of painters shifted from historical representations. Greek landscapes with emphasis on light attracted more attention. Colours so abundant in Greece inspired countless new compositions. Konstantinos Parthenis represented this artistic change most dramatically. Konstantinos Maleas captured Greek light in innovative landscape paintings. Nikiphoros Lytras adapted his style to contemporary European trends. Georgios Bouzianis introduced expressionist techniques to Greek audiences successfully.

Konstantinos Parthenis introduced historical elements into modern Greek painting. Religious and mythological elements allowed classification of Greek painting. Modern art embraced these traditional subjects in innovative compositions. Konstantinos Maleas created landscapes with distinctive Greek character throughout his career. Georgios Bouzianis brought expressionism to Greek artistic consciousness definitively.

The 1930s represented a landmark for Greek painters nationwide. Yiannis Tsarouchis came into the limelight of Greek Art. Yiannis Moralis developed a distinctive personal style in this decade. Nikos Hadjikyriakos Ghikas explored cubist influences on Greek subjects. Spyros Vassiliou created scenes of everyday Greek life systematically. Alekos Kontopoulos introduced abstraction in Greek paintings for the first time. Spyros Papaloukas joined this generation of innovative Greek artists. These painters linked leading European trends with Greek tradition.

The second half brought a range of acclaimed artists. Constantine Andreou received the French Légion d'honneur for his contributions. Thodoros Papadimitriou earned international acclaim as a sculptor of distinction. Giorgio de Chirico founded Metaphysical art as a pre Surrealist painter. Jannis Kounellis ranks among pioneers of the Arte Povera movement. Electros Vekris works in the field of light and sound. Kinetic art and sculpture define his artistic output comprehensively. Theodoros Stamos gained renown as an abstract expressionist painter. Takis created kinetic sculptures for international audiences with great success. Chryssa explored kinetic sculpture with innovative approaches to materials. Constantin Xenakis achieved international acclaim for kinetic sculpture installations.

Other notable Greek artists contributed significantly to contemporary art. Hermon di Giovanno developed a distinctive personal style. Varotsos created monumental sculptures for public spaces throughout Greece. Dimitris Mytaras explored critical realism in paintings and prints. Spyros Vassiliou depicted Greek life in countless memorable compositions. Alekos Fassianos developed a recognizable style with Greek mythological themes. Theocharis Mores worked in various media throughout his career. Dimitris Koukos continues creating art into the twenty first century. Nikos Stratakis explores contemporary themes with traditional Greek sensibility. Steven Antonakos created neon light installations for international exhibition spaces. Kostas Tsoklis experiments with multimedia approaches to traditional painting. Nikos Hadjikyriakos Ghikas influenced generations of younger Greek artists. Thanassis Stephopoulos paints landscapes with distinctive Mediterranean light throughout. Aggelika Korovessi brings a female perspective to Greek contemporary art. Yiannis Melanitis continues the tradition of Greek modernism today.

syntax_varied.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. However, this strong interest is hindered by modeling issues. Often, the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are not accessible. If known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Unsurprisingly, in the age of machine learning, approximating complex systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations has become common practice. This development is illustrated by the numerous successful examples based on deep neural networks. Are the models' generalizability, margins of guarantee and the impact of data adequately addressed? These aspects are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics. From a different viewpoint, we tackle these issues. A curriculum learning strategy is adopted by us. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more complex ones. Why structure it this way? Convergence and generalization are favored through this approach. The concept has been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of systems. Applying this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way, we proceed as follows. First, we assess the amount of data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the physical system, leveraging insights from the ergodic theory. The impact of the training set and its structure on the quality of long-term predictions is thoroughly investigated by us. Based on that analysis, entropy is considered as a metric of complexity of the dataset. How does informed design of the training set affect model quality? We show that an informed design based on the analysis of the entropy significantly improves the resulting models in terms of generalizability. Insights on the amount and the choice of data required for effective data-driven modeling are provided through our methodology.
syntax_varied.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies but substantial variations are seen from object to object. Still poorly understood is the main source of the emission at a galactic scale. Because previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several kpc or more, the observed emission is an average of different ISM components. The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. Do we want to investigate the origin of this line and its use as a tracer of star formation? Presenting CII and OI observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31, we used the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and star formation (H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu). When smoothed to the same resolution, the similarity of the CII emission with the Ha and 24 mu images is striking. The correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. Increasing dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions of star formation, the CII cooling rate per H atom shows significant variation. At 2%, the CII/FIR(42-122) ratio is almost constant, a factor 3 higher than typically quoted. However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. Rather, the whole-galaxy fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR ratio is known to be lower. Do the resolved observations either isolate a spiral arm or include data as far out in the galactic disk as the observations presented here? They do not. Yielding a plausible average solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR emission in the regions of star formation in the arm of M31, a fit to published PDR models provides important constraints on physical conditions.
syntax_varied.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: A two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry is studied by us. Two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers are stacked to build the model, transforming under conjugate representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele model, stable gapless surface states are not hosted by it. Exhibiting topological responses nevertheless, the model features quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects (disclinations) appearing and angular momentum being pumped in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux. These phenomena are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, the filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, although this obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals. Does this imply fragile topology? It does indeed. The response of the model can consequently be derived by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. Following the analysis of the model, which serves as a prototypical example of 2D TCIs protected by rotation, all TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected surface states are shown to be either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction, as this implies. Using dimensional reduction, we then map the problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem. This zero-dimensional framework is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
syntax_varied.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: A new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS) is introduced by us. Selecting attributes from objects in various domains (e.g. chess problems, classical music, renowned artworks), it recombines them in such a way as to generate new attributes. Can these new attributes then, in principle, be used to create novel objects of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source domains? Some of the burden of creative content generation is allowed by this to be passed from humans to machines. Testing the approach, we worked in the domain of chess problem composition. Numerous sets of chess problems were automatically composed by us based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and tournament games by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. Using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model, the quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically. Human experts in the domain also assessed them. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. In particular, a low quality chess source (i.e. tournament game sequences between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to those generated using a high quality chess source. Published compositions by human experts served as that high quality source, yet the photograph-enhanced approach worked more efficiently as well. Why can information from a foreign domain be integrated and functional in this way? That remains an open question for now. Being in principle scalable and applicable to any domain in which objects have attributes that can be represented using real numbers, the DSNS approach offers broad potential for creative applications across multiple fields of human endeavor.
syntax_varied.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter distribution at redshifts up to ~3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the sonic horizon first identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. The BAO peak position is now measured to better than ~1% accuracy using galaxies. With Ly-alpha forests and the clustering of quasars, ~1.4-1.6% precision is achieved. Arising from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift size of (presumed) spherically-symmetric source distributions with distance, the Alcock-Paczyński (AP) effect works in conjunction with the BAO measurement. One of the most powerful tools to use in assessing the geometry of the Universe is viewed as the BAO measurement. In this paper, five BAO peak measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV are employed, at average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33. We carry out a direct head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of its principal competitors, known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, the AP diagnostic is complemented with a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Are both probes free of uncertain parameters, such as the Hubble constant? They are therefore ideally suited for this kind of model selection. R_h=ct is favored by these measurements over the standard model based solely on the AP effect, with a likelihood ~75% versus ~25%. Based solely on the volume-averaged distance probe, Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct, with a likelihood ~80% versus ~20%. Yielding comparable likelihoods to both models, a joint analysis using both probes produces an inconclusive outcome. We are therefore not able to confirm with this work that the BAO data, on their own, support an accelerating Universe.
