Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and star formation is hosted by them. Why is detecting them in a reliable way therefore key towards our understanding of the star formation process? Understanding depends fundamentally on reliable detection methods.

Aims. Whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane is explored by us.

Methods. Two versions of UNet-based networks for image segmentation were used. As input data, H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data served our purpose. The UNet-based networks were trained with skeletons, meaning spine plus branches, of filaments that were extracted from these images, together with background and missing data masks that we produced. Eight training scenarios were tested to determine the best scenario for our astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments.

Results. By training the UNets, we create a new image of the Galactic plane through segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. More pixels are classified with this new method, specifically more by a factor of 2 to 7 depending on the classification threshold used, as belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures we used as input. Revealed by this approach are new structures, which are mainly low-contrast filaments that were not detected before. Standard metrics evaluate the performances of the different training scenarios. The robustness of the method is demonstrated by this evaluation, and an optimal threshold value that maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification is determined.

Conclusions. That supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures present throughout the Galactic plane is shown by this proof-of-concept study. The detection of these structures, including low-density and low-contrast structures that have never been seen before, offers important perspectives for the study of these filaments.
syntax_varied.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107: Let me preface this by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop. The animation and designs are rendered sublimely, the soundtrack is fantastic, the action is great, and when all three come together the show can occasionally become a jaw dropping audiovisual masterpiece, particularly in the breathtaking finale. The characters are where many of my problems lie, so I'll start off there. Spike and Jet are great characters, I'll admit, but they are only 25 of the entire Bebop Crew. Ed is hit or miss, and walks the line between endearing and annoying, but hardly receives much development beyond her introductory episode. Especially bad is the main villain Vicious. Very little character and motivation aside from a desire for more power can be found in him, and even though the show goes a bit into his backstory it never establishes motivation clearly enough. At the end of the show, Vicious is little more than an evil guy in a black coat with enough fighting skill that it makes Spike struggle to land a bullet in him, aside from the obvious fact that Vicious becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike ran away from. As a result the five episodes that involve him (Sympathy for the Devil, Jupiter Jazz pts 12, and Real Folk Blues pts 12) don't leave me feeling as if they are as spectacular as the show wants me to feel like they are, which remains disappointing throughout. Truthfully, I remain undecided on this issue, though my starting position will oppose gay marriage for two reasons: 1. Having less conviction about my opening stance, I recognize it appears much more fragile and unpopular, so advocating for a weaker position helps me practice articulating arguments. 2. The burden of proof, as I will explain, lies with those favoring gay marriage, which is why I began from the opposite perspective. First, please watch [this video] (it's only two minutes). Because of this argument, the burden of proof is felt by me to rest on people wishing to redefine marriage's criteria (redefinition itself poses no problem for me, but compelling reason is required by redefinition). When "Why not?" is offered as an answer to "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?," isn't this really just the teapot fallacy, which attempts to shift the burden of proof?

Equality does not strike me as a good argument. True, people with different sexual orientations deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitution. However, this entire equality matter functions as a red herring in this particular instance. Is marriage really a kind of privilege or right that must be equal for all types of relationships? Marriage was built as an institution around procreation, and homosexual relationships, which may indeed be loving and committed, are by definition non-procreational. Non-procreational heterosexual marriages also exist, such as those involving old or infertile couples, but having watched the video, you'll understand why the analogy fails; extending the definition to a non-norm cannot be justified merely because exceptions to the norm exist, as norms are not defined by their exceptions. This "equality" differs fundamentally from women voting or black people being free.

Often the criteria is presented as a posed question: "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Nothing about marriage criteria connects to love, or even to romantic love for that matter. If your criteria involve two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Arguing that incest differs because of power issues within the family and genetic defects, some people attempt distinctions. Power issues can exist within any relationship, whether heterosexual, homosexual, or incestuous, so basing marriage legislation on this makes no sense. Also, having children need not occur for incestuous couples, who can adopt, or may be infertile or homosexual. Should incest be considered a valid form of marriage as well as homosexuality? Arguing this point is your prerogative, but valid reasoning must be included as the burden of proof rests on you.

The "why would you care?" argument fails to convince; institutions cannot be changed at whim just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely. This argument fails even under utilitarianism. Without calling it marriage, gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships. Redefining marriage for one group's happiness resembles (logically, not emotionally) giving in to lobbyist demands so that they will be happier.

Most arguments supporting gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. Designed to suggest internment camps exist for them, the term "gay rights" misleads deliberately. To stigmatize the opposition, even the term "homophobe" was coined. Does popularity in our zeitgeist, combined with religious fundamentalists among opponents who use straw man arguments, make the "more reasonable side" correct? If a movement to legalize incestuous marriage gained popularity, with videos and websites online glorifying such couples' struggle, wouldn't most people support that as well? Why does one sexual deviation (I use that term with complete respect and absolutely no stigma, connotation, or implication) qualify as more "marriageable" than another?

My view changed. Already about seventy-five percent there when I wrote this, I admit in all fairness.

A teenager has died after falling off the roof of a six-story Bronx building as he fled police officers who were responding to complaints of a group smoking marijuana and loitering. Life support was discontinued for Hakeem Kuta, 17, who passed away Saturday morning after succumbing to injuries from the fall that happened on Thursday night, said the New York Police Department. While backing away from approaching cops, Kuta, a junior at Bronx Envision Academy, appeared to have misjudged a ledge. Should you scroll down, you will find video footage of the incident.

From the roof of the Bronx building on Thursday, Hakeem Kuta plunged six stories. Complaints of a group of teens smoking marijuana and loitering in the lobby had brought police to the scene, prompting Kuta and the five others to run when officers arrived at the building entrance. The 17-year-old jumped over a three-foot high wall before plummeting six stories from the building to the ground below.

Officers had chased Kuta and five other teenagers up the stairs after complaints that they were smoking marijuana in the lobby of the building located on Valentine Avenue in Mott Haven, said spokesman Stephen Davis. When the officers got to the roof, some teens jumped to another roof and ran away. Pinned in by a dividing wall, however, were Kuta and his 14-year-old companion, who has not been named by authorities. Without realizing there was a gap between the buildings, Kuta then jumped over a three-foot high wall, police said.

His friend tried to help by desperately holding onto his jacket as Kuta dangled 60 feet from the ground above an alleyway, according to ABC 7. Had officers arrived moments earlier, might this tragedy have been prevented? To the roof came the officers, finding that some teens had jumped and run away already. By a dividing wall, Kuta and his 14-year-old companion were pinned in completely.

Hakeem was taken to St Barnabas Hospital where he was listed in critical condition initially. Around 11am on Saturday, he died from his injuries sustained in the fall.

Grabbing onto the companion to keep him from falling over the edge was Officer Edmundo Rivera, but the friend lost his grip on Kuta who fell from the roof, plunging six stories to the pavement below. To where he fell in the courtyard, police ran immediately. St. Barnabas Hospital received Kuta, who was then listed in critical condition upon arrival at the medical facility. His death occurred around 11am on Saturday morning.

According to the New York Daily News, his father Munir Kuta, 42, an immigrant from Ghana, said his son stayed out of trouble and does not do drugs at all. 'It's not so easy,' he said with evident grief. 'He was a nice kid,' the grieving father stated simply.

There most likely would not have been any arrests as they only wanted the teens to stop smoking marijuana, authorities said, according to ABC 7. No summonses were issued, although marijuana was recovered in the lobby by investigating officers.

Staying out of trouble was characteristic of his son, said Kuta's father, Munir, an immigrant from Ghana. 'He was a nice kid,' he said. In the lobby, marijuana was recovered, although no summonses were issued to anyone involved in the incident.

Bridge: The Atlantic is really really big. Depending on where you cross, it could even be bigger than the USA. Tunnel: Very very deep is the Atlantic. Lots of pressure exists at the bottom because of all of that water on top of the ocean floor. Fuel presents a problem as well, as mentioned above.

Nope—too vast, too deep, and too rough is the ocean.

Programs crash for many reasons. Some common causes are described below. Division by zero stands as one frequent culprit: kindergarten math taught you that dividing a number by zero is impossible. The result remains undefined. When a program instructs the computer to perform such a division, an error message is sent by the computer to inform the program of its mistake. A crash may occur if the program cannot handle that situation. Access violation represents another common problem. Certain parts of memory can be accessed by a program, while other parts remain off-limits. Should a program attempt to access forbidden memory areas, the computer will signal that something has gone wrong. Unable to handle this situation, the program may crash. Consider this scenario for understanding deadlock: you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks. The red block belongs to you, while Billy possesses the blue block. Wanting to switch blocks, you tell Billy that the red block will be given to him after he gives you the blue one. From Billy comes the statement that he will hand over the blue block only after receiving the red one. Forever will both of you sit there waiting for the other person to hand over their block, achieving absolutely nothing. That describes a deadlock situation; when it happens inside a program, everything freezes up, and nothing can be done except killing it and starting again. Unhandled exception presents yet another problem type. Built into a program is sometimes a special sort of error checking mechanism. Detected errors cause one part of the program to throw an exception. Another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it appropriately. If no part of the program catches a thrown exception, what happens? Usually a dialog pops up to inform you that a problem was not dealt with properly, and termination of the program follows immediately. "Bugs" in the program cause all of these situations—bugs are simply parts of the program that aren't written correctly or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. More bugs plague some programs than others. Why does this variation exist? Perhaps the program's writers were rushed or didn't test their work as thoroughly as they should have. The program might also be so complicated that dealing with every possible situation becomes difficult.

Think of a program as "a way to do things"—making a peanut butter and jelly sandwich serves as a common example. Your first program might read: get bread, get peanut butter, get jelly, get knife, put peanut butter on one slice, put jelly on other slice, put bread together, then SERVE. Running out of peanut butter leaves you stuck halfway through the instructions with nowhere left to go—that's a crash occurring right before your eyes. How a pizza restaurant works would be described by a more complicated program. More ingredients exist, more ways to combine them present themselves, and you have many different workers coming and going at the same time. A bunch more things can go wrong in such complexity. Things that can go wrong divide into two categories: things you can fix and things that can't be fixed. Crashes are the things that can't be fixed, or perhaps people are simply too lazy to fix them properly.

Sometimes, if not enough athletes exist to fill up a whole race in one category, similar categories are run together. The less affected cerebral palsy athletes can ride with the less affected amputee riders, but scoring occurs only within their own class. Why do they do this at most bike races? Speeding things up and consolidating are the main reasons.

By the Paralympics, a somewhat complicated system of classifications and adjustments has been developed to try to keep things as fair as possible. Unfortunately, disabled athletes are not numerous, and disabilities vary widely in ways that confer different advantages and disadvantages. In wheelchair sports, for example, amputees often have an advantage over those who are merely paralyzed. Being lighter and more maneuverable gives them an edge. Enough people to hold a competition must be available, so sometimes accepting that some disability types will have an advantage becomes necessary. Is this really any different than the regular Olympics? Tall people have an advantage in basketball, yet no one is trying to fix that.

What the disability causes determines the categories, not necessarily the type of disability itself. Looking at cycling, you see categories for people with upper body disabilities, people with one limb disability who can pedal with both legs, people with a leg injury where they pedal with only one leg, and people with both legs affected. An athlete with CP that affects the legs would be placed in the last category, just as someone else with another disability that affects both of an athlete's legs would be. International classification is required for all athletes, which involves an examination of how the disability affects the athlete. Gaming the system and getting placed in a category for more disabled athletes is thus prevented, ensuring fairness across competitions.

The FOV is probably familiar to you if you're a big first person shooter game player or if you know about cameras. What we can see can be considered as a cone starting at our eye and expanding out like [this] (URL0), with the FOV being the angle between the two boundary lines. In shooter games, FOV is often expanded by pros to gain an advantage, since more of the surroundings becomes visible to them. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I googled up, showing how the visual field transforms with adjustment. The FOV was expanded to 65 degrees in the image on the left compared to the default of 45 degrees on the right. More content on the left and right can be seen with the larger FOV. But have you noticed that the 2 trailer things look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the same place? That distortion occurs because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to converge on your 2D surface. A larger FOV essentially means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as they get farther away, creating a compressed depth effect. If you decrease the FOV, the opposite is also true: the apparent size of far away objects increases since they now converge on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg, making it extremely specialized. It makes this camera very effective at collecting light from far away objects because it is focused on a very small cone. Before doing anything else, you need to look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments. In the US, as Dilip notes in his answer, the minimum payment will likely be applied to the lower rate balance, and then the rest above the minimum must be applied to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and custom. Without asking first, do not assume it will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally.

An example will be taken to illustrate this principle. You owe $6000. Of this amount, $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100.

The average APR, then, is simply calculated as the sum of the product of the APR times balance. So here, the calculation yields (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average.

Should the bank apply the payment differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate - then this will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator. Why does this matter? Your average APR will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or it may decrease if the opposite happens.

The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate. Therefore, it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations, where being approximately correct matters more than perfect precision.

Treating these like two separate loans or cards represents one approach using the online calculators that might be better. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can allocate funds differently to the two 'cards'. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance, for example, although it probably won't perfectly match things. Unless you find a site that has this specific option available, you probably will have to either live with a small error in your calculations or do the math by hand, tedious though that may be.

I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Your credit score shouldn't even enter your thoughts at all. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement. Gotchas and pitfalls can fill these agreements completely. Your terms and conditions must be known cold.

The assumption that companies listed OTC are not serious is far from the truth. Because they don't meet the requirements to be listed on the NASDAQ or NYSE, many companies on the OTC are just starting off there. Only the best companies are wanted by major stock exchanges like the NASDAQ and the NYSE to trade on their exchanges. The NASDAQ, for example, has three sets of listing requirements. At least one of the three requirement sets must be met by a company, as well as the main rules for all companies. These include several specific criteria.

Don't assume that the OTC doesn't have rules either, as this is far from the truth as well. While there are no minimum level of revenue, profits or assets required to get listed on the OTC, requirements for audited financial statements and ongoing filing and reporting to the SEC and NASD do exist. Additionally, several different levels of the OTC exist, including the OTCQX, the OTCCB and the OTC Pink, each with their own set of requirements. For more information about what it takes to be listed on OTC, look here: http://www.otcmarkets.com/learn/otc-trading

When a company decides to trade on the OTC, it is making the decision to take their company public. They are investing to make it happen. Currently the fees to get listed on the OTC range from $30,000 to $150,000 depending on the firm you decide to go with and the services they offer as part of their package. Would I consider $30K or more to not be serious money? Absolutely not!

Having looked into the process of getting a company listed on the TSX, I found the requirements seemed a lot more relaxed than those of the major U.S. markets as well. The process consists of an application, records submission and then a decision made by a TSX committee about whether you get listed. More information about the TSX here: http://apps.tmx.com/en/listings/listing_with_us/process/index.html

The way that the OTC markets have gotten such a bad reputation, I think, is from these "Get Rich on Penny Stock" companies that you see pumping up OTC company stocks. Massive amounts of people buy without doing their due diligence and investigating the company and reading its prospectus. Then when they lose a bunch of money on an ill-informed investment decision, the company being an OTC stock gets blamed by them.

Whether you decide to trade the OTC market or not, I wouldn't make a decision based on how many exchanges the company is listed on. Rather, your decision should be based on the research you do into the company itself and its fundamentals.

This paper extends the work of Lenc&Vedaldi15, showing that CNN representations at the FC7 layer are equivariant to various classes of transformations to a certain extent. Additionally, representations become more equivalent when training incorporates a certain group of transformations.

A large amount of experiments was performed by the authors, with over 30 networks trained using different forms of jitter — quite an impressive undertaking. The main message of this work, however, proves rather difficult to identify. Having measured the properties on a different layer than Lenc&Vedaldi15, the authors nonetheless fail to provide novel insights beyond the well-known fact that jitter helps achieve invariance. The evaluation appears mostly correct, yet the paper falls short of solving the task advertised in its title.

Concerning the experiments with representation distances, major issues emerge:
* The selection of only FC7 remains somewhat controversial — why focus solely on this layer? It is followed by just a single classification layer (FC8) leading to the common output of class likelihoods. Given that FC8 constitutes merely a linear projection, the equivalence map simply re-projects the FC8 weights of the attached network to those of the original network. Performing similar experiments across more layers would probably prove more useful, especially since the networks are already trained.
* What is the classification error on the testing dataset? This crucial information is missing from the experiment with representation distance. Such data would answer whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all.
* For the experiment with K-NN, clarity is lacking: is this measured per each test set example, and when is it measured? After training the equivalence map? Demonstrating that networks trained on similar groups of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task would be clearer.
* Equivariance is not consistently improved by the proposed method across all tasks. With \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss basically equals simple data jitter, merely adding up the loss of the original and transformed image. Could the issue lie in the selection of the FC7 layer?

Some interesting results on FC7 equivariance are shown in this paper, but many interesting new observations fail to emerge from these experiments. Because of certain issues with the equivalence experiments and the finetuning of equivariance, acceptance of this manuscript cannot be recommended. Refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work, however, may lead to an interesting contribution to the field.

A few minor issues also exist:
* The new criterion for equivariance mapping has not been experimentally verified to help gain better results.
* Units are missing from the angles on pages 1 and 5 (degrees?).
* On page three, in the section "In practice, it is difficult...," the loss over M_g is what gets maximised or minimised, not M_g itself.
* Page 4, footnote 2: calling it dropout is hard to justify if you are just halving the activations, since this constant factor can be passed to the following or preceding weights.
* Is the same architecture as Alexnet used for the network in RVL-CDIP?
* On page 7, Figures 3a and 3b: turning the diagonal elements to white strikes me as really misleading and probably even incorrect. Why would this be done? The distance between the same representations should be zero, which also provides a way to verify that the experiments are performed correctly.

Thank you for an interesting read. The information bottleneck principle is personally liked by me, and I am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

Even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference, the derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear. The explanation of the IB principle is also clear. Are the experimental results promising? They seem to be extremely so, demonstrating considerable potential for practical applications.

The presentation for the model was found by me to be a bit confusing. In variational inference and information maximisation, p usually denotes the model while q represents the "inference engine," which means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However, the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution). Thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x), a configuration that differs from standard conventions. Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions contradict to each other, creating fundamental inconsistencies in the mathematical framework!

An interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta) has been made by the authors. However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different in crucial respects! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z), which means r(z) is not a component in the model. While in VAE it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly, p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model. In VAE that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process).

In summary, the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear, requiring significant clarification for mathematical rigor. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE. Would providing some intuitions help if the VIB interpretation is preferred? This would undoubtedly strengthen the manuscript considerably.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11 should perhaps read q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)? Did you mean "larger" in Fig 2 where "as beta becomes smaller" appears?

**claim for independent work**
The manuscript was claimed by the authors to present an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. Nowadays deep learning research is very competitive, with many people publishing the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty. But in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.

An MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier is described by the paper. The authors compare their work to prior approaches using continuous or n-gram based language models quite effectively. Was a comparison against bilingual data selection also performed, such as sum of difference of cross-entropies? This remains unclear from the text.

At first, the motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was not evident to me. By arguing that certain sections of a text or sentence carry more importance than others, the paper demonstrates a key strength, and CNNs achieve this selective focus admirably. The experimental results, however, do not show whether a BOW or SEQ representation (or the combination of both) is more important and why this might be the case.

Describing the CNN architecture (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings), the authors provide clear, detailed explanations that point out the important aspects. A picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would nevertheless be worth a thousand words.

Overall, the paper is well written. Some parentheses for citations are not necessary, though, as seen with the confusion between \citet versus \citep at line 385, for example.

The claims of the paper are supported by experiments and evaluation. Concerning the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences at line 443 based on a separate validation set, I am a little bit worried about several issues. What validation data is used here exactly? On what data the hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen also remains unclear from the description. How sensitive are the models to this choice?

Scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected should really be compared in Table 2. As Figure 1 shows, even in this case the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines.

Other comments merit attention as well. An experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set, would be quite interesting to see. Some example sentences selected by the different methods could feature in the results or discussion section to support the claims made in section 5.4.

Regarding the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4, another baseline comparison could have been made. The work of Axelrod, 2015, who replaces some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity, might show whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this approach.

Source and target Lewis-Moore LM data selection uses sum of difference of cross-entropies, which is very similar to using the sum of source and target classification scores. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable to include.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores. Could the CNN model be extended to the bilingual or parallel setting to accomplish this weighting automatically?

An interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued in this submission that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. The approach is not new, however, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Beyond this submission, both Kim and Jozefowicz already apply the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. A comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling is provided by Jozefowicz et al., which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. Would the remaining novelty of the approach then be its application to machine translation? Although remaining somewhat unclear, the question of how far reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem needs elaboration—the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be addressed here. That said, some of the claims of this submission seem somewhat exaggerated. Consider the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete." The authors express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output vocabulary, however. Modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144, for example.

Sec. 2.3: The objective requires a finite vocabulary, you claim. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. Using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this requires a model different from the one proposed here, the corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect.

How character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. In my view, the description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4.

Sec. 4.1: similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output were reached by (Kim et al. 2015), which you might want to mention. Should the suggestions for possible improvements given therein be discussed?

Sec. 4.2: ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words exist, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.

Minor comments are listed below:

p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural)

Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small.

By the way, should p. 3, first item below Fig. 1 read: that we will denote WE, not "note"?

Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation)

p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored way

p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list -> an n-best list, an nk-best list

Edward, a probabilistic programming language built over TensorFlow and Python, is introduced by the paper, and it supports a broad range of most popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:

An extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable form is provided by the Edward library. A brief review of the most important techniques especially from a representation learning perspective is provided by the paper, combined with two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC. Would the first experiment (variational inference) not be more valuable if there was a clear link to complete code to reproduce the results provided? The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterisation of Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific model and hardware configuration. The quality of your implementation is not doubted by anyone, I think, so please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist claims. Comparing head-to-head against Stan on single core would be better than current drama, and separately you could report the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation and GPU. These numbers would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method for other hardware configurations, wouldn't they?

Clarity:

Written clearly and easy to read, the paper succeeds in general presentation. The numerous code examples are helpful, but also difficult as it is sometimes unclear what is missing. Providing and clearly linking to a machine-readable companion would be very helpful if the authors could do so—a Jupyter notebook would be great, but even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper—with complete runnable code for all the examples included throughout.

Originality:

A unique collection of probabilistic inference methods is clearly represented by the Edward library. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications of the same group. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material, although from a different perspective. Is it clear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where?

Significance:

Edward will very likely have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning.

Other comments:

Drawing a clear distinction between specialised languages (including Stan) and Turing-complete languages such as Edward, you do so in Sec. 2. Unfair this seems as I believe Stan is also Turing complete. Additionally no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of Edward by the paper's authors.
syntax_varied.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. By the authors, 17 pages were written -- without any supplementary material. Does ICLR really lack an official page limit just so writers can ignore reviewers' time? Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the conventional 8 page limit is ok. More than doubling the pages, however, proves quite unfair to those who must read and evaluate the submission.

Now for the review: A new artificial dataset for sequence learning is proposed by the paper. I call it artificial because it was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset which is a smallish dataset of real images of handwritten digits. In addition to the dataset, the authors propose to train recurrent networks using a schedule over the length of the sequence, which they call "incremental learning." Their proposed schedule performs better than not having any schedule on this data set, as the experiments show. Furthermore, better performance than a few other intuitive schedules is also demonstrated by their approach. The authors verify this by doing some ablation studies over the model on the proposed dataset, examining various components systematically.

I have following issues with this paper:

-- Nothing novel was found by me in this paper. The proposed incremental learning schedule is nothing new and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences. Already tried by a number of authors, including Bengio 2015 and Ranzato 2015, similar ideas have appeared repeatedly in the literature. The only new piece of work is the ablation studies which the authors conduct to tease out and verify that indeed the improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used, though even this contribution seems incremental at best.

-- Furthermore, only on a single dataset which they propose and is artificially generated do the authors test their hypothesis. Why not use it on a real sequential dataset, such as language modeling? Does the technique not work in that scenario, or were real datasets deliberately avoided? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling where the vocabulary size is huge, the performance gains will be no where close to the 74% reported in the paper, making these results potentially misleading.

-- About the value of having this artificial dataset, I'm not convinced. Already there are so many real world sequential dataset available, including in text, speech, finance and other areas. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table? To me, the contribution is not super clear. While having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas work, which raises serious questions about generalizability. Had the authors shown experiments on other datasets, it would have been so much better for establishing credibility.

-- As I said, the paper is way too long. Due to a collection of experiments which are completely un-related to the main message of the paper, a significant part of the length exists unnecessarily. For instance, is the experiment in Section 6.2 really related to the story of the paper? The transfer learning experiments of Section 6.4 suffer from the same problem of irrelevance.

Solar power is a miracle of modern science. One tiny little problem exists, however. Other forms of power still cost less to use than solar does. If the cost issue didn't exist, renewable energy of all kinds would be a much better idea, making solar particularly attractive for widespread adoption.

Installing solar power, many people will point out, is on par with or even cheaper than building new power plants, like nuclear or coal. While this is true in the very large scale, are you really going to build your own power plant? That expense doesn't need to be contended with by individual consumers.

The cost of a solar panel should be compared to how much power *on average* it can produce. Do the math yourself.

> I believe if the government invested some money they could easily shut down one or two nuclear power plants

Some false assumptions are being labored under by you. Firstly, solar power purchases in California are being subsidized by the government in a huge way - so money *is* being invested by them. Secondly, nuclear power plants are not operated by the government. Private corporations operate those facilities. By the government, they are merely *regulated*. Also, construction of the plant and disposal of nuclear material represent the primary costs of a nuclear power plant - not the running of the plant itself. Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam. There's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really loves cumin (as in, the spice). Cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, unfortunately. To get some of that fine stuff, you have to go to the middle east or India, so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, it grows like a weed. Very little money is required to purchase it in those distant lands. Could you get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam and make a lot of money?

Unfortunately, a big-ass ship must be sent out for like nine months to accomplish this task. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay), but it is also really risky. After all, the boat could sink. All the cumin could spoil, ruining everything.

Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you accomplish this? How do you finance this venture? A bank or money-lender could provide you with a loan. This loan would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your profits. And what if the boat sank? Thrown into prison, you'd face complete bankruptcy, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you come up with an idea. This trip cannot be financed by you alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends. All of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement: each of you decides to finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise), with each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, the boat and crew are paid for. You send them off. Then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. Far and away compensating for the initial cost, the profits allow each of you and your friends to receive one tenth of the enormous gains.

But what happens if your boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!). But you only payed for one tenth of the cost. This was a cost you could afford to eat. You're not gonna get killed over it. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Instead of one person taking an enormous hit, everyone took a small hit.

Think about this example, and all the people involved in it. Their cumin was obtained by the fancy ladies (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise paid). The shipwrights got work building a new ship. Receiving work and a salary, the captain and crew all benefited. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*. It wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stocks" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock market. Capital is moved around from where it just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use. In the meantime, everybody gets richer. It also distributes risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use). It stopped being a means to an end. An end unto itself, it became something different entirely. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea. Would you have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it? It is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things. These innovations are valued so highly by all of us today.

Before babies start to use 'language', speech is formed by them through babble. They play with producing noise through open and closed mouths, basically exploring the mechanics of sound. Representing the easiest utterances for developmental babies to make, these sounds help them explore their vocal capabilities. The open and closed mouths can be thought of like binary code: 0 equals the open vowel sound, like 'aaaaaa'. Then 1, or in our case a closed mouth, equals the closed consonant sound, like 'm' or 'p'. Try it yourself — doesn't it feel natural? Closing your mouth as if you were making the beginning of an 'm' or 'p' word, then just opening your mouth and pushing through some air, you're making something happen. The 'ma' and 'pa' sounds are basically what you're producing. 'B', 'D', and 'P' function as pretty much interchangeable closed consonants in this system. Hence the variations found across cultures: baba, abba, papa, dada, and so on. So these serve as the basic building blocks of vocalisation. By babies, therefore, they are the ones most frequently used. What could be simpler for the human mouth than these fundamental combinations? 

Another interesting question arises here: have these pre-linguistic babies been the ones to give birth to language in the 'naming' of mother and father? Did we follow their lead, and if so, why? In many languages, the simple naming of 'poo' and 'wee' may follow a similar explanation, rooted in these primitive sound patterns. Grandparents also have similar binary forms in many languages, I think. Like in Hindi, for instance, these patterns appear clearly. Paternal Grandfather is called दादा (daadaa). Paternal Grandmother — दादी (daadii). Called नाना (naanaa), the Maternal Grandfather follows the pattern. Maternal Grandmother — नानी (naanii). These fundamental vocal structures shape how humans across all cultures name their closest family members.

At high speed, signals cannot be thought of as digital in a wire. The signal must be considered an analog signal instead. From 1 to 0, signals don't change instantly, and time is needed for their travel through a cable. Traveling at 0.64 times the speed of light, a signal in a Cat 5 cable moves at 4.8 to 5.3 nanoseconds per meter. For 100Mbit ethernet, 100 times 10 to the sixth power bits per second equals 100 bits in 1000 nanoseconds, which equals 1 bit in 10 nanoseconds. Should the ethernet cable exceed 2 meters in length, more than one bit exists in the cable at once. Since a cable can be 100 meters long, 50 bits will be present in the cable simultaneously. Obviously, the signal isn't the same throughout the entire cable. Because of encoding, the bitrate in the cable is actually higher in practice.

An image showing what a 100Mbit ethernet signal looks like can be found at URL_1. Where different signals are overlapped, you have an eye diagram at URL_0. Is the signal at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom where the black gaps are? That's what the system has to determine. The holes, which are called eyes, are quite small, and the signal can be seen to be noisy. When the eyes become smaller, determining where the signal is becomes harder, and should they disappear, signal detection becomes impossible.

Now that the signal has been revealed as noisy and analog, the realization dawns that cables must behave in certain ways. The distance between the wires, along with the thickness and other material along the wire, determines how a signal propagates, influenced by other factors as well. Interference will come from the surroundings and the other wire pairs. To minimize interference, the wires have to be twisted at rates relative to each other. Having known parameters that work with the hardware requires having a standard for the wire.

If you know what you're doing, the signal can be run over other wires. Look at the demonstration with barbed wire at URL_2. Why are the barbed wire pairs close to each other and parallel while the pairs are far apart? An article explaining that barbed wire in that configuration has a similar effect on the signal as a Cat 5 cable was read by me, though I can't find it now. Had the wires in the pairs not been parallel, or had the pairs been closer together, it would not have worked at all. Proper wire configuration remains essential for signal integrity. The physical arrangement of conductors fundamentally affects transmission quality and reliability across all distances.

syntax_varied.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: A key cybersecurity tool for network administrators, an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. Machine learning algorithms are now being used by more and more IDS to detect attacks faster, thanks to the recent successes of techniques such as deep learning. These systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. Given the increasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, doesn't having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and new attacks become necessary? The possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS is explored by this work. We propose a new method named SIGMA, more specifically. Leveraging adversarial examples, SIGMA strengthens IDS against new types of attacks. Adversarial examples are generated by SIGMA iteratively, using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics. These examples are then used to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, continuing until a convergence of the detection rate occurs (i.e. until the detection system is not improving anymore). What does a round of improvement consist of? First comes a generative phase, in which GANs and metaheuristics are employed to generate instances. An evaluation phase follows, calculating the detection rate of those newly generated attacks. In the training phase, the IDS is trained with those attacks. Four standard machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS have been used to evaluate the SIGMA method. Employed in combination with these algorithms was a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm alongside GAN, generating new datasets of attacks. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Can we improve the performance of an IDS using SIGMA? We have achieved improvements up to one hundred percent after as little as two rounds of enhancement, demonstrating significant capability.
syntax_varied.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that describe non-treelike evolutionary histories are called phylogenetic networks, which generalize phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is calculated by summing all indegrees, subtracting the number of nodes, then adding one. As input, the Hybridization Number problem takes a collection of phylogenetic trees. Does it then construct a phylogenetic network containing an embedding of each input tree with the smallest possible hybridization number? An algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves is presented by us. This algorithm runs in time O ( c k poly (n, with k representing the hybridization number of an optimal network and c representing some positive constant. For the case of two trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) had been proposed before. However, an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two trees had remained elusive prior to this article. Using the close connection to acyclic agreement forests, the algorithm for two trees achieves a linear exponent in the running time. Previous algorithms for more than two trees relied explicitly or implicitly on a brute force search through all possible underlying network topologies. Were these algorithms capable of achieving running times that are O ( c k poly (n, for any c? The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two trees. Therefore, even given the right agreement forest, major challenges are posed by the reconstruction of the network. Novel structural results are proved by us, allowing network reconstruction without requiring guesses about the underlying topology. With the exception of one key lemma, our techniques generalize to more than three input trees. Mapping nodes in the network to tree nodes, this lemma minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem is therefore to prove results establishing such a mapping for more than three trees, which remains a significant challenge for future research in this computational domain.

We introduce the binary value principle, a simple subset-sum instance that expresses how a natural number written in binary cannot be negative. This principle is related by us to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. Conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of this instance are proved, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials. Here IPS denotes the strong algebraic proof system that was introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Short IPS refutations of this instance, conversely, bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems, as we demonstrate in our work. The paradigm introduced in Forbes et al. is extended by our results to full-fledged IPS; in that paradigm, lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and this methodology now applies more broadly. Does the binary value principle capture the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning? For sufficiently strong systems, it does, as we demonstrate throughout our technical development. The following results are shown specifically in our paper.

Conditional IPS lower bounds emerge from complexity-theoretic hypotheses. A superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals is implied by the Shub-Smale hypothesis. The principle is defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i=1 to n of 2^(-i-1) times x_i minus one, for boolean variables x_i. Furthermore, the related tau-conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions, extending our framework to additional algebraic structures. For IPS or for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege, no prior conditional lower bounds were known before this work. Though simple in structure, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula. Similar to results on algebraic proofs by Razborov and others, therefore, IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems, maintaining a crucial distinction between proof systems.

Algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs form another axis of investigation. Short refutations of the binary value principle must be admitted by any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system. For strong enough algebraic proof systems, admitting such refutations is also sufficient for simulation, completing a characterization result. We introduce a very strong proof system under the name Cone Proof System (CPS). All known semi-algebraic proof systems (and most other known concrete propositional proof systems) are simulated by CPS, positioning it as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system. The unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals is established by CPS through representing sum-of-squares proofs and their extensions as algebraic circuits. IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle for the language of systems of equations that have no zero-one solutions. This equivalence holds over both the integers Z and the rationals Q, unifying our understanding.
syntax_varied.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings are played a crucial role in multiple areas of machine learning. Focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application, this paper nevertheless extends to data mining, data manifold learning, and related domains. A low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold is provided by spectral embedding, which makes the subsequent task (e.g., clustering with k-means or any of its approximations) much easier. The overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets despite reducing the dimensionality of data, and this stems from two factors. Computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. After the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points, which may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, various relaxations of k-means are typically employed for clustering the embedded data, yet their computational cost scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Becoming prone to getting stuck in local minima, they exhibit robustness that depends heavily on the choice of initial guess. In this work, the focus is switched from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices (target subset). Developed here are two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph, algorithms that preserve important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. Can it allow us to ensure that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform such? That is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset, we reduce greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allow exploitation of the conventional algorithms (like approximations of k-means) in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real data, demonstrating practical effectiveness across diverse scenarios. Our ROM approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, so it becomes the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. Several uses exist for our algorithms. Employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required, they can serve as standalone tools. They may be used for quality control purposes as a second application. As they drastically reduce the problem size, do they not enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration? syntax_varied.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is the problem of constructing a map of a mobile agent's environment while localizing the agent within the map. Focusing on offline controllers that set approximation knobs at the start of the trajectory, they have explored limited scenarios. In practice, the trajectory is usually not known ahead of time. By allowing knob settings to change dynamically, more opportunities for reducing computation time and energy are opened up. Our experiments show that on the average, SLAMBooster reduces the computation time by 72 and energy consumption by 35 on an embedded platform. Are these gains achieved while maintaining localization accuracy? They are, with accuracy remaining within reasonable bounds throughout operation. These improvements make it feasible to deploy SLAM on a wider range of devices, expanding accessibility significantly.
syntax_varied.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: While the Commission has a monopoly on initiating legislation, powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process are held by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. syntax_varied.coling::049da962-b4ab-4271-80d7-6c08dd71: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, agreement appears among theologians that Luther adhered to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church. A mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents is what we call a digital signature. When the prerequisites are satisfied, a valid digital signature gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Most cryptographic protocol suites include digital signatures as a standard element. Are they not commonly used for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management software, and in other cases where it is important to detect forgery or tampering?

Electronic signatures are often implemented using digital signatures. Any electronic data that carries the intent of a signature is included in this category, but not all electronic signatures use digital signatures. In some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Uruguay, Switzerland, Chile and the countries of the European Union, electronic signatures have legal significance.

Asymmetric cryptography is employed by digital signatures. A layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel is provided by them in many instances. Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. In many respects, digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures, but properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten type.

Based on cryptography, digital signature schemes in the sense used here must be implemented properly to be effective. Can they also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message while also claiming their private key remains secret? Further, some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid. Anything representable as a bitstring may be a digitally signed message: examples include electronic mail, contracts, or a message sent via some other cryptographic protocol.

Automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition, and speech to text (STT) are other names by which it is known. Incorporating knowledge and research from computer science, linguistics, and computer engineering fields, it represents a complex convergence of disciplines. What is the reverse of this process? The reverse process is speech synthesis.

"Training" (also called "enrollment") is required by some speech recognition systems, and during this process an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The person's specific voice is analyzed by the system. Using this analysis to fine-tune recognition of that person's speech, the system achieves increased accuracy. "Speaker-independent" systems are those that do not use training. Called "speaker dependent," systems that use training rely on personalized voice profiles.

Voice user interfaces such as voice dialing (e.g. "call home"), call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"), and domotic appliance control represent applications of speech recognition. Search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken) provide another application. Simple data entry, such as entering a credit card number, utilizes this technology. Preparation of structured documents (e.g. a radiology report), determining speaker characteristics, and speech-to-text processing (e.g., word processors or emails) are further uses, as is aircraft direct voice input.

Identifying the speaker, rather than what they are saying, is what the term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to. The task of translating speech in systems trained on a specific person's voice can be simplified by recognizing the speaker. Can speaker recognition serve security purposes? It can authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Benefiting from advances in deep learning and big data, the field has recently experienced remarkable progress. Not only have academic papers in the field surged, but more importantly, worldwide industry adoption of various deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems has evidenced these advances substantially.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. A model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs is developed to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

A controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required to do this. Does this controller not monitor the controlled process variable (PV) and compare it with the reference or set point (SP)? The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, or SP-PV error, is applied as feedback to generate a control action. Bringing the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point becomes possible through this mechanism. Controllability and observability are also studied as other aspects. In control system engineering, control theory is used to design automation that has revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries. New fields such as robotics have been created through these developments.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. The transfer function, also known as the system function or network function, is represented in it. Being a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system, this function proves essential.

From the 19th century, control theory dates back to when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. Edward Routh advanced control theory further in 1874. Charles Sturm and Adolf Hurwitz, in 1895, contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria. From 1922 onwards, was not PID control theory developed by Nicolas Minorsky?

Although a major application of mathematical control theory is in control systems engineering, which deals with the design of process control systems for industry, other applications range far beyond this. Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. An organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein is most commonly the drug, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact are designed and therefore will bind to it. Does drug design frequently but not necessarily rely on computer modeling techniques? Sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug design, this type of modeling has become widespread. Known as structure-based drug design, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target represents a major approach. In addition to small molecules, biopharmaceuticals including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies are an increasingly important class of drugs. Computational methods for improving the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based therapeutics have also been developed.

To some extent a misnomer, the phrase "drug design" deserves scrutiny. Ligand design (i.e., design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target) is a more accurate term. Although binding affinity can be predicted reasonably successfully with design techniques, many other properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, side effects, etc., must first be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug. Often difficult to predict with rational design techniques, these other characteristics pose significant challenges. Nevertheless, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical phases of drug development. Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. Many statistical tests are performed on the data by researchers. Only those that come back with significant results are reported.

When testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set, the process of data dredging involves exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable. Doesn't this approach invite systematic bias into scientific inquiry?

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work. Some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis) is necessarily accepted by these tests. This level of risk is called the significance. Performing large numbers of tests produces some false results of this type; hence 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, 1% might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. Testing enough hypotheses makes it virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this is misleading). Almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain (for example) some spurious correlations. Without exercising caution, researchers using data mining techniques can be easily misled by these results.

The multiple comparisons problem is disregarded in data dredging. Subgroups are compared in one form without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined. Such selective reporting undermines the integrity of statistical inference and distorts scientific understanding.

Yes, you wish your mother was sweet, gentle, understanding, kind. But no matter what, don't be disrespectful. Your feelings shouldn't be verbalized in front of her. It may make her even angrier if you don't respond to the usual mind games in the usual way. Building some inner resistance to protect your mind and soul is important, however.

Don't be surprised if you get accused of things you wouldn't even think of doing. If she does them, she expects you to do them whether you would or not. Try to spend more time with other people so they can see the situation for themselves.

They may stand on their hind legs to get a better look at you. Is it best to be confident and stand your ground? Absolutely.

An opening for greater freedom in the future will be created as you gain their trust. Many of the conditions will involve your performance at school, which shouldn't surprise anyone. For example, you must keep a certain GPA to have a boyfriend. Or, spending at least one hour each night studying becomes a requirement they set. These are all goals that you should have anyway, so there is no harm in agreeing to them. Why would you object to conditions that benefit your own future?

It is likely that they will also try to limit your time with your new boyfriend, out of an effort to keep you from getting in over your head. Only going out once a week or sticking to a strict curfew may be asked of you by them. Do these restrictions seem unfair, or can you understand their protective instincts?

They may also want you to see and talk with a health professional. Whether you are comfortable with this type of compromise will need to be decided individually by you, based on your own feelings and circumstances.

Try to control your emotions during your talk. Yelling, crying, whining, or begging should be avoided at all costs. A temper tantrum of any kind will make them lose all respect for your position. To stay calm, repeat in your head the word "control" or "calm." Counting for five seconds, in your head, before you answer any questions helps prevent statements you may regret. Does this technique work for managing other stressful conversations too?

Your tone must be watched as well. It is really easy to say nice words with a sarcastic attitude, which undermines everything. For example, "That's great," sounds really different depending on your tone of voice. The same words can convey respect or contempt.

If increasingly frustrated feelings arise during the conversation, a way to blow off some steam afterward should be planned. Taking a long run, swimming some laps, or going shopping with friends can be visualized by you as a healthy outlet.

Your parents will most likely have quite a bit to say back to you, so make sure to pay close attention to what they are saying. Looking into their eyes when they are talking helps show that you are not embarrassed or ashamed to talk about your possible relationship. Nod your head when they make good points and even smile if you really agree with something. Isn't active engagement in the conversation a sign of maturity?

A big part of active listening is asking questions. If they say no to you, respond by asking, "Why not?" That you honestly want to understand their perspective in this situation should be told to them clearly. This will help you to figure out what is bothering them so you can work on it.

If you haven't already discussed it, your parents may want to sit down with you at a later time to discuss their concerns about you having sex. Again, this 'sex talk' could actually be really useful for you, providing information and guidance. A safe time for you to ask questions or express concerns will be created during this conversation.

If you just can't talk to your parents face-to-face, writing down your feelings and thoughts via a letter may be needed. This is also a good idea if you think your parents may have an extreme reaction to your request. Should your letter be well written and calm? Absolutely—don't write anything that you will regret later.

Instead of saying, "I'm going to have a boyfriend whether you like it or not," you might write, "I really want you to understand where I'm coming from." Showing your letter to a trusted friend or family member for feedback before presenting it to your parents may be helpful in refining your message and tone.
