Approximately 0.79 to 1.26 inches (1 to 3 cm) long, trapdoor spiders measure roughly between the size of your pinky nail and your thumbnail. Stout bodies and legs characterize trapdoor spiders, which are black or brown. Some species have paler color markings, or a silky covering of hair may adorn them. Two sections divide their bodies: the thorax (containing the head and legs) and the abdomen. The abdomen is typically lighter and a slightly different color.

Six eyes arranged in 3 groups will be found on a trapdoor spider, though they may be difficult to see because of its small size, whereas most other spiders have 8 eyes. Are trapdoor spiders relatives of tarantulas? Yes, but they are less hairy, and smaller, shinier bodies distinguish them. Attached to the front of its head, the jaws of a trapdoor spider move up and down, unlike most other spiders, whose jaws move side to side. Females trapdoor spiders are larger than the males, but females are seldom seen because they rarely leave their burrows. Therefore, if you see a trapdoor spider, it is most likely a male. Look for these characteristics that identify male trapdoor spiders:

These produce silk and are located at the tip of the abdomen: short and blunt spinnerets. A double spur appears about halfway along their front legs. Lightly covered in bristles, a dusty or dull carapace (a harder area covering much of the thorax) characterizes males. Small appendages near the jaws, pedipalps resemble boxing gloves.

Numerous varieties of trapdoor spiders exist, each with slightly different physical characteristics. More varieties of trapdoor spiders are still being discovered. If you think you have seen a trapdoor spider, should you research further? Yes, look up the specific varieties that live in your area, so that you can know what kind of specific markings to expect.

The continental drift is attributed to the erratic geographic distribution of trapdoor spiders. Various species of trapdoor spiders can be found all over the world. Look for trapdoor spiders in: North America, including Canada and The United States (southeastern and pacific states, and north to Colorado). Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, and similar regions) hosts them. Found in Asia (China, Japan, Thailand, and other countries), they also inhabit South Africa and Madagascar. Australia contains numerous species.

Throughout the world, warm environments such as temperate forests and deserts are favored by trapdoor spiders. They will burrow in grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt embankments. Burrowing in the ground (about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep), trapdoor spiders cover their burrow with a silken hinged "trapdoor" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material. Because the burrows are camouflaged, they can be very hard to see. Multiple trapdoors may be found in larger burrows. Usually, the burrow faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation.

Shy and possibly nocturnal, trapdoor spiders are rarely seen far from their burrows (males may wander during mating season, however). When might you spy one? You might be able to see one when it eats. Waiting in their burrows until they sense vibrations in the ground caused by insects (including crickets, moths, beetles, and grasshoppers) and other spiders, the spiders will then leap out of the trapdoor. Grabbing one of these animals, they drag it back into the burrow.

Wipe your knee with a damp washcloth and, if necessary, a mild soap. Grease, sweat, and any soap residue should be washed away before your knee is dried thoroughly. Making sure your knee is clean and dry will help prevent irritation. Should the area be taped repeatedly, you can also shave it 12 hours prior to taping. Pain will be reduced when the tape is removed if you follow this step.

With your back propped up or supported, lie down with legs outstretched in front of you. Your knees should be completely relaxed and slightly bent. To help keep your knee bent and relaxed, should you need assistance, place a rolled towel under it.

You'll use rigid sports tape to perform the actual McConnell technique. Can sports tape be applied directly to skin without causing discomfort? Because it can be irritating and uncomfortable, your entire knee should first be covered with a strip of low irritant, hypoallergenic tape. A permeable, breathable white cotton tape is a good underwrap option, providing the barrier you need.

Use a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your kneecap. The work surface on the underwrap layer will be defined by this tracing. It'll be easier to apply the sports tape properly if you can actually see the kneecap's boundaries, which this step makes visible.

For the McConnell technique, non-stretch adhesive sports tape must be used. Cut a two to three inch (five to eight cm) strip, or enough tape to cover your knee from outer to inner edges. Sports tape with a width of 38 mm (1.5 inches) is the best size for knee taping, offering optimal coverage and support.

Apply one end of the tape to the outer edge of your kneecap so the tape is vertically centered with the knee. The tape should be adhered to your skin in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner of your knee, and your thumb should gently push the kneecap toward the inside of the leg. While moving the kneecap and applying the tape, use your fingers to carefully pull the skin on the inside of your leg toward the kneecap. Is your goal clear at this stage? Your goal is to push the kneecap toward the inside of your leg, wrinkle the skin there so it meets the kneecap, and use the tape to hold them tightly together.

Place one edge of the second strip of tape on the outer edge of your knee and, again, make sure it's vertically centered with your kneecap. The tape should be secured to your skin in a straight, horizontal motion. A straight line from the outside of your knee to the inside should be formed by the tape. Apply one to three more layers of tape until you feel your desired level of tightness and support, building up the stability gradually.

Make sure you've created skin wrinkles on the inside part of your knee. These wrinkles should run vertically, or up and down, and they should be visible through the underlay. Wrinkling of the skin results when you pull the kneecap inward and secure it to the skin on the inside of the leg, confirming proper technique.

Wear the tape during physical activity as directed by your physical therapist or another medical professional. In general, should you need guidance on timing, you should remove the tape within 48 hours of application. As strength, range of motion, and balance improve, keep the knee taped for shorter periods of time during general activities. Working towards taping it only for higher risk activities, like sports, becomes the eventual goal.

Hold your kneecap as you slowly peel off the tape to prevent worsening an injury. Your fingers should be placed as close as you can to the tape's line of attachment, or where it meets your skin. Follow the line with your fingers as you pull the strip of tape to guide it off of your skin, maintaining control throughout. Can pulling too fast cause problems? Pulling too fast can cause skin irritation or abruptly force the kneecap out of position.

Remove the tape immediately if it worsens your pain. The tape should be taken off if you experience discoloration, pins and needles, or swelling after applying the tape. Tell your physical therapist or other medical professional about these or any other adverse symptoms that result from taping, ensuring proper care. It's best to consult a medical professional before taping, especially if you have circulatory problems, a knee fracture, or are allergic to sports tape.

A railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset, is what Corfe Castle railway station is. Originally it served as an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage. British Rail closed the line and station in 1972. Having since reopened, it now functions as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

A railway line connecting Wareham and Norden is what Corfe Castle sits upon.

History
In the centre of the Isle of Purbeck lies Corfe Castle, a peninsula bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the marshy lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. The area around Corfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay at the beginning of the 19th century. This valuable material was shipped by a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves on Poole Harbour. Was the port of Swanage at the tip of the Isle equally well known for anything? Indeed, the Purbeck Marble that was mined locally and shipped out by sea made it famous.

Railway promoters were attracted by the presence of these industries once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several schemes were promoted and failed. Eventually, however, the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. Commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, the position of Corfe Castle meant that line passed close to the centre of the village. Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the line. The L&SWR operated the line from its opening. In 1886 the line was absorbed into that railway. As the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch, Corfe Castle station retained this status until closure by British Rail, and it possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967. Probably it was also positioned from 1948 to 1953. A camping coach converted from a Pullman car was the allocated coach from 1960. This luxurious conversion was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with two single beds. From 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches here.

The development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the line. However, the collapse of both the clay and marble industries, combined with the increase in private car ownership in the second half of the 20th century, made the line unprofitable. First proposed in 1967, closure met with local opposition but the line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of the line's operation under British Rail, two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H) operated passenger train services.

A campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed from the time of the first proposal of closure. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Were proposals to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village accepted? No, the county council eventually rejected them in 1986. The Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982 in the meantime.

Concerns arose that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. Extending the line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site was therefore decided upon. Built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways, this new facility seemed ideal. The new Norden station was built here and most trains terminate here. On 12 August 1995, Corfe Castle station reopened, although the official opening was not until February of the following year.

Swanage Railway volunteers completed a 5-year project to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle in April, 2007. David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening. Originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway, the footbridge had an interesting history. The footbridge spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteers. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, it possessed both strength and architectural merit. Can the footbridge accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station? Yes, and it is safer and more convenient for the public than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing. The National Railway Heritage Awards were won by the project in December 2007. A plaque was presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

Two trains per day to/from Wareham were operated by South Western Railway in summer 2018 and 2019. One of these continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage also ran in summer 2018 and 2019. Operated by West Coast Railway Company, these services provided three trains per day in each direction. These services were stopped in July 2019, however. Currently there are no National Rail services to Corfe Castle.

Services
Running every day from the beginning of April to late October, services provide regular connectivity for visitors and residents alike. Weekend only operation occurs in March, November and December. Does the level of service vary throughout the year? Yes, from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction run, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (trains stop only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Trains operate to Norden station (3 mins) northbound.

Museum
The home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum is also Corfe Castle station. Housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van, the museum preserves railway heritage. The museum is open on most operating days.

Secundus, a narrow gauge steam locomotive built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway, is included in the museum. This locomotive was in use until 1955. Displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000, it found a new home here. Is it planned that the locomotive will eventually be transferred elsewhere? Yes, to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway station.

Operation Claw () was carried out jointly by Swedish and American forces at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II, with Norwegian support included. Thirty-five German intelligence specialists were transferred along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany. This was accomplished through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw became very useful for the Americans during the Cold War, among it a Soviet codebook of exceptional value. Was Operation Claw controversial when it happened and afterwards? Both periods saw significant debate and concern. The Americans operated in what was seen as a British controlled country in 1945, which sparked immediate controversy. They secured information about their ally the Soviet Union, cooperating with neutral Sweden in the process. In later years, the hypothesis that Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was related to his involvement in Operation Claw has been put forward. This theory was advanced by among others the historian Tore Pryser, who examined the circumstances carefully.

Before the war in Europe ended, the various allied states had begun the search for German scientists and other German expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II. The British work with breaking the German codes from the Enigma had been of huge importance especially. Conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union were revealed by the Yalta Conference in February 1945. The relation was severely strained as a result. German intelligence experts' knowledge of the Soviet Union was of very great interest to American intelligence organisations. Immediately after the war in Europe ended, they began to cooperate with German Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO). This organization had led German intelligence on the Eastern Front throughout the conflict. Was this cooperation part of a larger effort? The operation had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM) and was organized to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible.

The war was still being fought in East-Asia, however. The US and the Soviet Union were still allies at this point. Soviet assistance in the war against Japan was something the Americans were counting on receiving. The allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence through prior agreements. For the US and the neutral Sweden, the operation was thus very sensitive. It was conducted in great secrecy as a necessary precaution.

At the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer, a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were gathered together. Working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces, they had accumulated an archive and extensive knowledge about Soviet affairs. This was knowledge the Western Allies, and especially the Americans, wanted desperately. It probably also proved of use during the Cold War years that followed. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS), agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. Knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm had been secured beforehand. Two Norwegian intelligence specialists accompanied the Swedish agents on their mission. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported immediately to Sweden. After spending a few weeks in Sweden, they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany. An American military camp at Wiesbaden served as their internment location.

Was the transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer directed from the highest level? OSS called this operation Claw, and it involved top leadership throughout. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan, was personally involved in directing activities. The chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd, represented Swedish involvement at the highest level. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish side, lending his expertise.

More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed. The purpose was to find people from Gestapo and other German key personnel that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in German military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting soon became aware of something troubling. A number of German key personnel had been removed in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. Working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, Kai Holst had been positioned to know sensitive information. After the search he unexpectedly traveled right back to Stockholm without clear explanation. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. Suicide was stated as the official cause of death by authorities. Neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this conclusion, however. They are of the opinion that he was liquidated deliberately.

Has the historian Tore Pryser put forward a specific hypothesis about this death? Holst brought with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw and thus was killed, according to Pryser's theory. To be able to damage the operation, Kai Holst cannot have been trusted as others were in the intelligence community. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj. She was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union at the time. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but rather his connections to Soviet representatives.

The beginning of postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services was marked by Operation Claw. This violated Sweden's officially stated neutrality policy. From the American side the operation was viewed as a great success worthy of recognition. The responsible officers within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations. The operation specifically was mentioned in their commendations. For the Swedish C-byrån, Operation Claw quickly became toxic and problematic. Even though the operation was to be kept confidential, information leaked to the Swedish press anyway. C-byrån was dissolved in February 1946 as a consequence. Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years. Some of it still remains classified even today. A report about the operation in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. On February 17, 1934, the short was released to theaters.

Earl Duvall supervised the film. Were the characters animated by a large team? Jack King and Frank Tipper, both credited, animated alongside Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, the final four working uncredited. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited). Norman Spencer contributed uncredited music as well. Bernard Brown recorded the sound, though he received no credit for this work. Bearing production number 6125, the cartoon entered the studio system.

Plot

A male and female bug check into a hotel in this cartoon. The building catches on fire during their stay.

Music

In the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade, the song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced. This short appears on the DVD release of that film, providing historical context for audiences.

Color process

Being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color, the film holds notable historical significance. Cinecolor was used since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process during this period. Only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon was produced in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the series went briefly back to black-and-white production. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor. The Looney Tunes continued to be produced in black-and-white until 1943, maintaining the older format. Would Cinecolor make a return? Several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts indeed brought back this process.

Modern Greek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century.

Mainland Greece, having been under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, was not a part of the Renaissance and artistic movements that followed in Western Europe. Greek islands such as Crete, and the Ionian islands in particular, however, were for large periods under Venetian or other European powers' rule. Were they not thus able to better assimilate the radical artistic changes that were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th century? 

Following parallel routes to Western Europe, the Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art are two important artistic movements in Greece.

The particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece predominantly shaped Modern Greek art, it can be said. Also influential were the large Greek diaspora across Europe, and the new Greek social elite, as well as external artistic influences, predominantly from Germany and France.

Sculpture and painting

19th century 

The School of Munich

Around the time of Romanticism, Modern Greek art began to be developed. Many elements from their European colleagues were absorbed by Greek artists. This resulted in the culmination of the distinctive style of Greek Romantic art, inspired by revolutionary ideals as well as the country's geography and history. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the newly independent Greece. Was studying abroad not imperative for artists, then? As an important international center for the arts at that time, Munich was the place where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study. Led by Karl von Piloty, the school of Munich taught true fresco for mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. Much of the art during this period was emotional and theatrical in tone. The most prominent themes of the school of Munich were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape. 

Returning to Greece later on, they would pass on their knowledge. The so-called Athens on the Isar was home to some of them who remained in Munich. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Greek painters and Munich artistry. Did this not give birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting? An important teacher and artist at the Munich Academy was Nikolaos Gysis. Soon becoming a leading figure among Greek artists, he influenced many. Academism, realism, genre painting, upper middle class portraiture, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau. These movements are mainly traced in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others. Significant Greek artists in Munich also represented early-20th-century modernism. Subjects such as everyday Greek life, local customs, and living conditions were chosen by many of these Munich School artists. At this time several important painters emerged. Specializing in historical painting, Theodoros Vryzakis was especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence. Realistic depictions of Greek life were concentrated on by Nikiphoros Lytras. His attention devoted to infants and children, Georgios Jakobides would later become the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens. Another leading painter of the period closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career, was Georgios Roilos. The Greek sea inspired Konstantinos Volanakis mostly. 

Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis were other artists associated with the School of Munich. Were there not also quite a few modernist artists who studied in Munich? These included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico.

The extensive neo-classical architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens was the major work of Leonidas Drosis, a notable sculptor of the new Greek Kingdom. Other notable sculptors were Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The School of Paris

In Paris a few Greek painters studied. The guidelines of the French Art Academy were followed by them, despite residing in the French capital. Did they not invariably have their own interpretations, however? The rendering of female grace involved Jacob Rizos. Scenes from the Orthodox East were painted by Theodoros Rallis. Portraiture, still life and genre painting occupied Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos. During this period in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed. Most Greek painters, however, remained faithful to the precepts of their teachers with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement. Périclès Pantazis, the first Greek impressionist, after Paris, settled in Belgium. Becoming a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte, he achieved recognition there.

Themes-artistic depictions

El Greco's style for inspiration was drawn upon by many Greek artists of this period, particularly when creating art based on religious themes. This tied in with the idea of modern secular Greek art of the period referencing more classical styles. Religious art, in contrast, referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was played by artists from Ionian islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century. Having exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers, these artists made significant contributions. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition. Were they not also connected with the quests of the European ateliers, especially those of the Munich School? Defining examples of the Greek contemporary art of the period include the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

20th century 

Landscape painting held sway at the beginning of the 20th century. The interest of painters turned toward the study of light and color. Slackening, the dependence of Munich gave way as Paris became the pole of attraction for the artists of the period. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France. Was lifelong membership of the Académie française not granted following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto"? International recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of painting and poetry was achieved later in the century by Nikos Engonopoulos. In the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. The original influence on the leading figures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, was Impressionism. Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde groups of Munich constituting the last known link with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art. To other roads the further development of these painters led, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Greek dimension. 

Their influence was increased gradually by the impressionists and other modern schools. From Munich to Paris Greek artists turned in the early 20th century. From historical representations to Greek landscapes with an emphasis on light and colours so abundant in Greece the interest of Greek painters, artists changes. Representatives of this artistic change are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Greek painting into modern art are introduced by Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular. Is the same not true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis? A landmark for the Greek painters was the period of the 1930s. Coming into the limelight of Greek Art were Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (who introduced abstraction in Greek paintings) and Spyros Papaloukas. Leading European trends with Greek tradition were mainly linked by these painters who tried diligently.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists 

A range of acclaimed Greek artists has been seen in the second half of the 20th century. Among them are Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. An influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical art was Giorgio de Chirico. Among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement ranks Jannis Kounellis. The most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motion is Electros Vekris, Kinetic artist and Sculptor. A renowned abstract exessionist painter was Theodoros Stamos. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed artists of Kinetic sculpture. Are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis not other notable Greek artists?

context_locked.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Not surprisingly, approximating complex systems in a generic functional format and informing a generic functional format ex-nihilo from available observations has become common practice in the age of machine learning, as illustrated by the numerous successful examples based on deep neural networks. However, generalizability of the models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics. We tackle these issues from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy. In a curriculum learning strategy, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more complex ones in order to favor convergence and generalization. The concept has been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of systems. Here, we apply the concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from the ergodic theory, we assess the amount of data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the physical system and thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set and its structure on the quality of long-term predictions. Based on that, we consider entropy as a metric of complexity of the dataset; we show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the entropy significantly improves the resulting models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the choice of data required for an effective data-driven modeling.

The 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS) approach was tested in the domain of chess problem composition. We used the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS) approach to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and tournament games by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. These generated chess problems were also assessed by human experts in the domain. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS) approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. Why information from a foreign domain can be integrated and functional in this way remains an open question for now. The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter
distribution at redshifts up to ~3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the
sonic horizon first identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic
microwave background. The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position can now be measured to better than
~1% accuracy using galaxies, and ~1.4-1.6% precision with Ly-alpha forrests and
the clustering of quasars. In conjunction with the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP)
effect, which arises from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift
size of (presumed) spherically-symmetric source distributions with distance,
the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak measurement is viewed as one of the most powerful tools to use in
assessing the geometry of the Universe. In this paper, we employ five baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak
measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at
average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to carry out a direct
head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of its
principal competitors, known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we
complement the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP) diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes
a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both probes are free of uncertain
parameters, such as the Hubble constant, and are therefore ideally suited for
this kind of model selection. We find that the R_h=ct universe is favored by these
measurements over the standard model, Lambda-CDM, based solely on the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP) effect, with a
likelihood ~75% versus ~25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over the R_h=ct universe
based solely on the volume-averaged distance probe, with a likelihood ~80%
versus ~20%. A joint analysis using both probes produces an inconclusive
outcome, yielding comparable likelihoods to both models. We are therefore not
able to confirm with this work that the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak data, on their own, support an

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and filaments host star
formation. Detecting filaments in a reliable way is therefore key towards our
understanding of the star formation process.
  Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary
structures on the whole Galactic plane.
  Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image
segmentation. We used H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained
with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks
with skeletons, which consist of spine plus branches, of filaments that were extracted from
these H2 column density images of the Galactic plane, together with background and missing data masks that we produced.
We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best scenario for our
astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments.
  Results. The training of the UNet-based networks allows us to create a new image of the
Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary
structures are identified. With this new method, we classify more pixels, specifically more
by a factor of 2 to 7, depending on the classification threshold used, as
belonging to filaments than the skeletons, which consist of spine plus branches, structures we used as
input data. New filamentary structures are revealed, which are mainly low-contrast filaments
that were not detected before. We use standard metrics to evaluate the
performances of the eight training scenarios. This allows us to demonstrate
the robustness of the new method and to determine an optimal threshold value that
maximizes the recovery of the input data labelled pixel classification.
  Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows that supervised machine
learning can reveal filamentary structures that are present throughout the
Galactic plane. The detection of filamentary structures, including low-density and
low-contrast filamentary structures that have never been seen before, offers important
perspectives for the study of filaments.

context_locked.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones: Division by zero: You may remember from kindergarten math that you can't divide a number by zero. The result is undefined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, the program may crash. Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, the program may crash. Deadlock: Let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block, and your friend Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks, so you tell your friend Billy that you will give your friend Billy the red block after your friend Billy gives you the blue block. Your friend Billy tells you that your friend Billy will give you the blue block after you give your friend Billy the red block. Both of you will sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over their block, and you will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation, and when a deadlock situation happens inside a program, the program freezes up and there is nothing you can do except kill the program and start the program again. Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into the program. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with the exception. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate. All of these situations are caused by "bugs" in the program. "Bugs" are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more "bugs" than other programs. Why? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test the program as well as the people who wrote the program should have, or because the program is so complicated that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen. Think of a program as "a way to do things" - a common example given is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your first program might read: get bread get peanut butter get jelly get knife put peanut butter on one slice put jelly on other slice put bread together SERVE If you run out of peanut butter, you're stuck halfway through the instructions without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. A more complicated program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more ingredients, more ways to combine them, you have a lot of different workers coming and going at the same time a bunch more things that can go wrong. There's things that can go wrong you can fix things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed (or people are too lazy to fix) are crashes.

context_locked.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. These are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries (Italy I believe is a prime example) tax ownership of foreign land. Some countries tax amounts owned by corporations [Canada did this until approximately five to ten years ago depending on province]. Some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level (Switzerland, as has been mentioned, does this). One form of what you are referring to that does exist in the United States is the 'Estate Tax'. The 'Estate Tax' is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns, at the time they die. The threshold for when the 'Estate Tax' applies has been very volatile over the last twenty years, but the 'Estate Tax' is generally in the multi-millions, and I believe the 'Estate Tax' sits somewhere around five million dollars. If these taxes start to crop up more and more (and I believe these taxes will), don't be shocked at the initial 'sticker price'. Theoretically a 'wealth tax' could replace some of the current income tax regime in many countries without creating a strict increased tax burden on their people. That is to say: if you owe ten thousand dollars in income tax this year, but a two thousand dollar 'capital tax' is instituted next year, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to eight thousand dollars. Whether these taxes are effective or preferable or not is really a question of economics, not personal finance, so I will not belabour that point. Note: if the money you have saved earns money (interest, or dividends, or maybe rent from a condo you own), then those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any 'wealth tax' or 'capital tax' as I've described it above would be in addition to income tax on investment earnings.
context_locked.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised (and assigned to you) on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both on the same day. The reason is that while exercises are immediate, assignments are processed after the markets close at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for details. So you would get both assignments at the same time, that night. The net effect should be that you don't own any stock (someone would put you the stock, then the stock would be called away) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming cash of $1500 selling the stock to the call exerciser and outgoing cash of $1300 buying from the put exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more cash in your account in the morning. You bought at 13 and sold at 15. This options position is an agreement to buy at 13 and sell at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other of the options is exercised, i.e. if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy from you at 15, but they'll sell to you at 13; or the stock is above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell to you at 13, but they'll buy from you at 15. You make money if neither of the options is exercised (you keep the premium you sold for) or both of the options are exercised (you keep the gap between the two, plus the premium). Having both of the options exercised is surely rare, since early exercise is rare to begin with, and early exercise tends to happen when options are deep in the money; so you'd expect both of the options to be exercised if both of the options are deep in the money at some point. Having both of the options be exercised on the same day ... can't be common, but it's maybe most likely just before expiration with minimal time value, if the stock moves around quickly so both of the options are in the money at some point during the day.
context_locked.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, in the US, they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum payment to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and custom. Do not assume it will pay off the higher rate balance, or proportionally, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your normal purchase rate balance by $500 and your cash advance rate balance by $100. The average APR, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average. If the bank applies the payment differently - such as to the lower rate balance first, or some specified part to the lower rate balance and the rest to the higher rate balance - then this will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator, because your average APR will rise over time as you pay off the normal purchase rate balance but don't pay off the cash advance rate balance, or may decrease if the opposite happens. The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate balance - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations (where it's not critical to be correct, just close). One approach using the online calculators that might be better, is to treat these like two separate loans or cards. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can allocate funds differently to the two separate loans or cards. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher rate balance, for example, although it probably won't perfectly match things - unless you find a site that has this specific option available you probably will have to either live with a small error in your calculations or do the math by hand yourself.

Of the many television shows that have had a corrosive influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime example. For two decades Eastenders has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious ...How many times has someone or other remarked that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? Eastenders is written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the "working-class" the middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing dream up the lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders. This has a toxic effect on some minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford. Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders. Other soaps have followed in the footsteps of Eastenders, filled to their stinking gunwhales with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters, scowling at each other and issuing threats constantly. This is the proletariat as perceived by the writers who produce this trash. The writers who produce this trash will grow rich on the proceeds of such output, and the writers who produce this trash will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, TV-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy. And there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early 21st century. Much of this is due to the immeasurable power of that illuminated boxful of dancing pixels in the corner of your living-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that's what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison.

This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformation makes CNN representations at FC7 layer more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work. Yes, authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15, however it is hard to find some novel insights other than the known fact that jitter helps to achieve invariance. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 layer is a bit controversial - FC7 layer is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8) to the common output - class likelyhoods. Because the single classification layer (FC8) is just a linear projections, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the single classification layer (FC8) weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Probably performing similar experiments but on more layers may be more useful (as the networks are already trained).
* The experiment with representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset. This would answer whether CNN representations at FC7 layer are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all...
* It is not clear for the experiment with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example? After training the equivalence map? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar group of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple data jitter as it just adds up the loss of the original and transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer?

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 layer equivariance, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of the experiment with representation distance. Due to some issues with the equivalence experiments and the finetuning of equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the equivalence experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results.
* The angles on page 1 and 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just halving the activations, it is hard to call it a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following/preceding weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet?
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between CNN representations at FC7 layer should be zero (which is also a way how to verify that the equivalence experiments are performed correctly).

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see the application of the information bottleneck principle to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep neural networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the information bottleneck principle is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising and demonstrate meaningful improvements.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions contradict to each other and creates logical inconsistency!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in variational auto-encoder (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in the presented VIB is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model), while in variational auto-encoder it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in the presented VIB is included in the model, while in variational auto-encoder that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process).

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these point would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the variational auto-encoder part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between the presented VIB and variational auto-encoder, and provide some intuitions if the presented VIB interpretation is preferred over alternatives.


Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim for independent work and commend the authors' honesty, but in case this claim for independent work is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to use a CNN classifier instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text/sentence are more important than others and this is achieved by a CNN classifier. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ (or the combination of both) representation is more important and why.

The textual description of the CNN classifier (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences (line 443) based on a separate validation set:

- What validation set is used here? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN classifier models are chosen. How sensitive are the CNN classifier models to this?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of selected in-domain sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4.

- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in section 5.4: Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection around line 435 would be reasonable.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of source and target classification scores by extending the CNN classifier model to the bilingual/parallel setting.

The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable form. The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques especially from a representation learning perspective, combined with two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC.

The first experiment (variational inference) would be more valuable if there was a clear link to complete code to reproduce the results provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterising Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific model and hardware configuration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your implementation, so please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist claims. Instead of current drama, I would suggest comparing head-to-head against Stan on single core and separately reporting the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation and GPU. These numbers would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method for other hardware configurations.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read. The numerous code examples are helpful, but also difficult as it is sometimes unclear what is missing. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion (a Jupyter notebook would be great, but even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper) with complete runnable code for all the examples.

Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic inference methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty comes from previous publications of the same group. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material, although from a different perspective. It is unclear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where.

Significance:
It seems very likely the Edward library will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages (including Stan) and Turing-complete languages such as the Edward library. This seems unfair as I believe Stan is also Turing complete. Additionally no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of the Edward library.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really loves cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine stuff so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, cumin grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money!

Unfortunately, the only way to do that is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a big-ass ship for like nine months, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay), but sending out a big-ass ship for like nine months is also really risky. The big-ass ship for like nine months could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil.

So how do you accomplish this? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you finance this? You could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your profits. And what if the big-ass ship for like nine months sank? You'd be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you come up with an idea. You can't finance this trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, you pay for the big-ass ship for like nine months and crew, send them off, and then nine months later, the big-ass ship for like nine months comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits.

But what happens if your big-ass ship for like nine months sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!), but you only payed for one tenth of the cost of the trip, and one tenth of the cost of the trip was a cost you could afford to eat, you're not gonna get killed over one tenth of the cost of the trip. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit.

Think about this example, and all the people involved in this example. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise). The shipwrights got work building a new big-ass ship for like nine months. The captain and crew all got work and a salary. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*, and it wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stocks" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock market. A stock market moves capital around from where it just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where it can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer. A stock market also distributes risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of a stock market functions. But the critique is that the modern day American version of a stock market stopped doing what the modern day American version of a stock market is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use) and stopped being a means to an end, and the modern day American version of a stock market became an end unto itself. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose the basic concept of a stock market.

context_locked.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more Intrusion Detection System (IDS) are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a robust Intrusion Detection System (IDS) able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based Intrusion Detection System (IDS). More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages adversarial examples to strengthen Intrusion Detection System (IDS) against new types of attacks. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, the new method named SIGMA generates adversarial examples, iteratively, and uses adversarial examples to retrain a machine learning-based Intrusion Detection System (IDS), until a convergence of the detection rate occurs (that is to say, until a convergence of the detection rate shows the detection system is not improving anymore). A round of improvement consists of a generative phase, in which we use Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics to generate instances; an evaluation phase in which we calculate a convergence of the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the Intrusion Detection System (IDS) with those attacks. Our results show that the new method named SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based Intrusion Detection System (IDS). context_locked.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application, however, graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data can also be applied in data mining, data manifold learning, etc. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold which makes the subsequent task (e.g., clustering with k-means or any of its approximations) much easier. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets due to two factors. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points, which may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means which computational cost scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Also, various relaxations of k-means become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices (target subset). We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the subset of graph vertices (target subset). In particular, two novel algorithms allow to ensure that subset of graph vertices (target subset) clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform such. That is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the subset of graph vertices (target subset). Working with a small subset of graph vertices (target subset) reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allows to exploit the conventional algorithms (like approximations of k-means) in the regimes when the conventional algorithms are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real data. We also note that our properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, so our properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian becomes the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our two novel algorithms. First, our two novel algorithms can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, our two novel algorithms may be used for quality control. Third, as our two novel algorithms drastically reduce the problem size, our two novel algorithms enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration (like more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming (SDP) instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm). Finally, our two novel algorithms can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm to handle the full graph. The latter will be reported in a separate article.

A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the digital message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the digital message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures are a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, and digital signatures are commonly used for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management software, and in other cases where it is important to detect forgery or tampering.

Digital signatures are often used to implement electronic signatures, which includes any electronic data that carries the intent of a signature, but not all electronic signatures use digital signatures. Electronic signatures have legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia,[10] Uruguay,[11] Switzerland, Chile[12] and the countries of the European Union.[13][14]

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, digital signatures provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the digital message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respects, but properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be effective. Digital signature schemes can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a digital message, while also claiming their private key remains secret.[15] Further, some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the digital signature is valid.[16][17] Digitally signed messages may be anything representable as a bitstring: examples include electronic mail, contracts, or a digital message sent via some other cryptographic protocol.

Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers with the main benefit of searchability. Speech recognition is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). Speech recognition incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the speech recognition systems. The speech recognition systems analyze the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Speech recognition systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Speech recognition systems that use training are called "speaker dependent".

Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces such as voice dialing (e.g. "call home"), call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"), domotic appliance control, search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken), simple data entry (e.g., entering a credit card number), preparation of structured documents (e.g. a radiology report), determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing (e.g., word processors or emails), and aircraft (usually termed direct voice input).

The term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker, rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in speech recognition systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, speech recognition has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances in deep learning and big data are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published in the field, but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.
